title: A good - not great - effort
review:
Episode II was good - not great.

Before seeing Episode II, I watched Episode IV once more. It was interesting to hear the same lines again, but with the perspective of seeing Episode I - a lot of Old Ben Kenobi's remarks were much less cryptic.

More of the same happens here - we see what Boba Fett looks like, and what's underneath a Storm Trooper's helmet (although we'll need to see Episode III to confirm that Storm Troopers == Clone Troopers).

I truly like the way this (Episodes I-III) is shaping up - like Memento (Christopher Nolan, 2000), our knowledge of the future shapes how we view the past -- moments of "Aha! Now I understand happened throughout the movie. Other people may be p***ed with this (e.g. my girlfriend feels that Boba Fett, like Inspector Gadget's Dr. Claw, should have never had his face revealed).

I await Anakin Skywalker's further descent into the Dark Side in Episode III...

Other comments

* the handling of C3P0 and R2-D2 was heavy handed - boy, did Anthony Daniels get some cheesy lines - probably to make the kids laugh.

* the robot factory scene - I found the most suspense there, as I anticipated (with the molten metal and the slicing machines) that Anakin was going to "get it".

* Lucas and team made Yoda too bouncy - settle down there Yoda!

* The romance scenes between Portman and Christensen were awkward - which I can excuse for Christensen, since he's playing a 16-year old. But Portman's way too frigid. Where's the fire, Natalie?

Conclusion

Episode I left a bad taste in my mouth. Episode II was a satisfying meal of a movie, well worth seeing. Suffer through Epsiode I and then see this one.

title: The Force is Strong
review: The force returns with a bang in Episode II, and the traditional elements that made the Star Wars saga so popular are here to savour. The film features the usual battle of good and evil, although this time there is a more sinister subtext which lends the film greater depth and emotional resonance. Although acting has never been the saga's strong point, the performances here serve their purposes and the characterisations are well rounded. With breathtaking action set pieces and awe inspiring visual effects, Lucas has put the saga back on track after the blandness of Episode I and sets things up nicely for Episode III.

title: Good and Bad
review:
I'm talking about the movie, not the characters. Since we've seen the results in the original trilogy, I didn't think there would be much suspense, as in the Phantom Menace. I was surprised.

I can't give out the details here, but from political intrigue to romantic subplot, Lucas partly redeemed himself by blending multiple story lines just like in Empire Strikes Back. What let this movie down, though, is the slow pace in many of the scenes. I especially detest the long race sequences. First few seconds, it was cool, but it gets old very fast, and I'm surprised anyone would like sitting minutes watching the same maneuvers over and over again. The action scenes were good, and the long wait is what made them even better. You learn so much about the characters.

Still, there's one more fault: Lucas is not a good writer when dealing with the "mundane." The initial scene between Anakin and Padme when the met again was so cheesy. Anakin has a habit of blurting out his feelings instead of letting us see him in action. This unsophisticated storytelling ruined a few scenes as a result.

This is a movie no Star Wars fan should miss. Then again, Lucas could have done a much better job, and we wouldn't have had to sit two and a half hours. It could easily have been a 100-min enrapturing blockbuster.

title: One of the BEst Sci-fi Films Ever
review: This is a quality film period.  I've read a number of reviews online criticizing the film since I've seen it.  In my opinion these are people going out of their way to put down the film.  I went in with no expectations and no plots already worked out in my head, and came out thinking the film was great. On another point, those puting down the CGI are talking rubbush.  I saw nothing wrong with it.  It all looks good.

title: The Force Returns
review:
I watched "The Phantom Menace" for the first time in a long time on May 16, just hours before going to see Episode II. I was pleasantly surprised. I thought perhaps that everyone (including myself) was unduly harsh in their criticism. Even Jar-Jar didn't seem all that bad. Then I went to see "Attack of the Clones"....

AOTC is so much better than its predecessor in so many ways. The acting, the visuals, the story, all are a major step up from the shaky Episode I. One may hear a lot of reviews complaining about terrible dialogue. It's nowhere near as bad as all that, perhaps because the main actors bring it to life so well. Ewan McGregor is quite splendid as Obi-Wan. One could sense great things in him in Episode I - here he is given much more to do. He has a wry sense of humour in some scenes that really endears himself to the audience, much more so than Hayden Christensen as Anakin Skywalker. Anakin starts showing the evil side of him that eventually leads him to become Darth Vader. Christensen pulls it off wonderfully. He is a very talented young actor, and shows off some impressive stuff in this one. His actions, and especially his reactions, during his most angry scene in the film (no spoilers here), are among the best of the entire series. And that brooding stare of his.....oooh. Speaking of "oooh", Natalie Portman is positively ravishing as Amadala. A fine performance also, but the sight of her in a midriff-baring white jump suit rivals Princess Leia in the metal bikini.

The story is surprisingly adult and complex. There is a genuine eroticism between Anakin and Padme. The splitting up of Obi-Wan and Anakin also gives the film a chance to develop two story lines. There is a real sense of intrigue about this film, the details of which must be seen to be enjoyed.

Of course, the visuals are immaculate. But that's what we all have come to expect from the Star Wars films, haven't we? What sets (and has always set) George Lucas apart form other sci-fi directors is that he never dwells on the settings or special effects. The impressive settings are given no more weight than if it was filmed on a city street or minimal location. I still feel that the new trilogy would be better suited with someone other than Lucas behind the camera, but this could be his best directorial effort yet. His innovative use of "hand held" camerawork for some of the digitally rendered fight scenes really legitimizes the vast amount of computer graphics in the film. They are so good that one doesn't even notice. Just sit back and enjoy the ride.

All this and I haven't even touched on Jar Jar Binks' cameo appearance, C-3P0 and R2-D2, and Yoda's memorable "performance". This film is on par with "The Empire Strikes Back" (both also have an awful title) in that it is much darker than the film it follows, and also much better. It also really sows the seeds of intrigue for the next one. Having watched "Attack of the Clones", Episode III could be the best Star Wars film ever.

See you in 2005.

title: *spoilers* good and bad of ep. II
review:
Where to begin? There were parts of AOTC that exceeded my expectations and other parts that fell far short of them.

If you struggle to see the good parts in Episode II, note Anakin confessing to Padme what happened at the Tusken Raider camp, think of how Boba is now linked in the Star Wars lore with the clones, or Anakin and Padme visiting the Lars homestead and Anakin sitting in the same place Luke sits in Ep. IV, or remember that plans for the Death Star have already begun.

For those who fail to see the bad in Episode II, I am forced to remind you of the purple lightsaber, the failure to show a real friendship between Obi-Wan and Anakin (Obi-Wan in Ep. IV: "And he was a good friend."), George Lucas's weakening ability to write dialogue (where's the man who wrote Yoda's advice to Luke in ep. V?), the choppy plot flow. And my biggest beef with the movie, which I'm sure I'll get used to, was Yoda's fight scene. Sure, in the heat of the movie it blew me away, but upon reflection, isn't Yoda powerful enough he doesn't even need to move to fight? Couldn't he duel Dooku with a lightsaber controlled by his mind. He even seemed swept away by his own abilities just as everyone was accusing Anakin of being. He was not the Jedi master who tells Luke, "Wars not make ones great."

Overall, I did like Attack of the Clones and eagerly await Episode III. I'm just disappointed at the realization that the new trilogy will never live up to the original.

title: Everything I expected
review: The Star Wars franchise is getting back on track, and Lucas is starting to get some of his old magic. I went to see this movie as soon as I could, because I was anticipating it so much, and I got what I expected. Note, I did not expect anything as good as the first trilogy. The plot was as strong as the first trilogy, and the acting was great (Hayden Cristensen does an excellent job, you can almost feel this dark energy flowing from him), but it seems that Lucas has lost his flair for dialogue and the love story seemed a little predictable and cheesy. The action scenes, however, more than made up for this. (I really got a kick out of the Crouching Tiger, Hidden Yoda stuff) This is not a love story, but it is a great action movie, and probably the best Star Wars "date" movie you could take someone to. It was what I expected, just don't expect too much.

title: Much better then I had thought it would be.
review:
Ep II proves again that Lucas should hire people to direct his screen plays. He just can't seem to get much out of an real actor. Beyond some flat parts on the dialogue and awkward "romantic" moments the sprit of the story was very good. What carried the film was the Special FX. Those FX people get a 10 hands down. ILM showed us, again, who the big dog of the movie FX world is. Hats off to modelers, animators, and hundred other people that pulled that off.

I wish Yoda would have said:

"Get medieval on your ass, I will"

title: Fantastic fantasy - back to what Star Wars should be
review:
Great fun, stunning effects, self-referencing humour, less Jar-Jar, exciting set pieces, Jango Fett and little son Boba, action galore and the trademark dodgy, unintentional sexual innuendo abound dialogue - this is what a Star Wars film should be.

While not in the league of Empire the film comes close to matching the glee with which generations have met the original Star Wars film, only falling short because 25 years of expectation and obsession don't allow Attack Of The Clones to match the originality of A New Hope in 1977. That said I don't see how any Star Wars fan, whether an obsessive fanatic or simply someone who has always just enjoyed the films as fun entertainment, could not like this film. With none of the flaws that Phantom Menace was accused of, even the scaled-down Jar Jar is less irritating, the film bodes well for Episode III.

Ewan McGregor is now much more comfortable as Obi-Wan and appears to be enjoying himself more. Natalie Portman looks stunning in an array of fanciful costumes. Hayden Christensen gives the sense of hidden anger you need in a character with his destiny. Christopher Lee continues to corner the market in fantasy saga villains - all those whispering "It's Saruman" to their friends will spend The Two Towers saying "Look it's Dooku".

Best of all however are the brilliant Ian McDiarmid as Chancellor Palpatine - the growth of this character was the best thing in Phantom Menace and is continued to great effect here - and the wonderful CG Yoda. I will not go into details but this film will leave you knowing why Yoda is THE jedi master after a scene that is, quite frankly, the crowning glory of the saga. It has been worth being a Star Wars fan for 25 years just for this scene. It is the pay-off with which George Lucas has rewarded his legions of followers.

Keep it up George, we now look forward to 2005 with renewed enthusiasm. See this film as soon as you can, it won't leave you disillusioned in the way Phantom Menace did many people. Attack Of The Clones is a wonderful entertainment, book your tickets today!

title: Positively AWFUL, far worse than Phantom Menace
review:
One of the most puzzling experiences I've ever had: when the credits came up at the end of the 12:05 AM showing of Episode II on opening night, the filled-to-capacity audience with whom I saw the film broke out in a huge ovation.

I can't for the life of me understand why.

Simply put, Episode II is a horrific movie. I mean awful. There is nary a single redeeming element to it. The CGI is obviously incredible and a sight to behold, but it is such a constant, dominant and overwhelming 'force' it literally began to blind me after a short time. Virtually nothing but the actors faces are real (I never thought I'd say that the made-up, surgically enhanced faces of Hollywood actors were the most realistic looking things in a film!) Special effects are great when they ENHANCE the visual movie experience, not when they replace it entirely. It's sort of like the off-Broadway theater piece Stomp, where several 'musicians' put on a concert using items like trash cans, sinks, etc. - anything but actual instruments. Initially, it's unbelievable, and you find yourself staring in shock at what these guys are able to do with common household items. But after about 20 minutes of cling-clanging, you find yourself praying they pull out a violin, or a piano, or a guitar, ANYTHING but another garbage can. Episode II is kinda the same way - the world is so computer generated, it simply blinds you.

The acting is absolutely atrocious. Everyone but Ewan McGregor (a fine, fine actor) and the two villains (Christopher Lee and Ian McDiarmid - thank goodness for the Brits) gives a bland to really bad performance. (Of course, with most of the characters being computer generated, that doesn't leave many other people.) Noteworthy for his particularly horrible acting is Hayden Christensen as Annakin Skywalker. This veteran of a lot of TV movies with the words "Love" and "Passion" in them couldn't even get the icky lovey-dovey scenes right (and there are an abundance of such nauseating, lean-on-the-shoulder-next-to-you-and-fall-asleep-while-waiting-for-the-ligh tsaber scenes in this flick), to say nothing of the wide range of feelings and the emotional 'journey' that the Darth Vader character expresses/goes through in this film. Christensen is at least consistent; he handles each scene equally poorly, looking more like a first year television acting student than the star of what will undoubtedly be the biggest grossing movie of all time. Much more so than the Phantom Menace, and even more of a focus than the action scenes, Attack of the Clones is a character-driven piece that focuses on the evolution of Annakin from Jedi to Darth Vader. You would think that if George Lucas chose to make that such a central theme he would've worked hard to ensure he cast a young actor capable of handling such a role. Why he chose to cast a pretty-boy with zero range is completely beyond me. Episode I came out around the same time as the Sixth Sense, the movie that catapulted young Haley Joel Osment's career, and for which he received universal acclaim for being such a highly skilled actor, despite his age. George Lucas, making the first installment in the biggest movie franchise in history, could've cast any kid in the world to play young Annakin, and he went with the decidedly mediocre Jake Lloyd. You'd have thought that he would've learned his lesson and made sure to cast the best possible actor this time around, especially in a movie in which the Vader role is so central. The fact that he chose to go with a flat pretty-boy shows he knows nothing about casting.

Oh, one more thing, this film is S-L-O-W. The battle scenes don't pick up until the latter third of the movie, until then the only thing to keep you awake is a painfully slow romantic development and a chase sequence in the beginning that goes on for about 45 minutes too long. The other primary focus of the first half of the movie is to drive into the audience's head, time and time again, over and over, the brewing "dark side" of Annakin Skywalker. Message to George: WE KNOW. We all saw the original trilogy. We all understand who Annakin is and what he will become. You don't have to have Christensen mysteriously "glowering" every couple of scenes, you don't have to repeatedly show him showing signs of selfishness, revenge and other non-Jedi traits, you don't have to show him breaking into fits of rage. WE KNOW. In Phantom Menace, the extent of the 'hinting' was that the Darth Vader music played once or twice when Annakin was on screen. This time, Lucas gives far less subtle 'hints' virtually every time Annakin appears on screen. It's overkill, it's unnecessary, it's annoying.

Overall, Clones is a terrible, terrible film. If you're a fan of light-saber action sequences, it's obviously well worth it. But if you wait until it comes out on DVD (yeah right), avoid the neck-cramp that will come from falling asleep on the chair and skip right through the first two thirds of this painfully bad film.

And please, if you find out what drug they put in the air that made everyone in the theater I saw it in hoot and holler, let me know what it is. Maybe we can package it and send it to Lucas so he can inject the next installment with a dose of energy and excitement.

title: Review
review:
***** WARNING! Possible Spoilers *******

I saw the latest (and dare I say greatest) chapter of the Star Wars Saga at 12:01am on opening day. Like some I found some flaws with TPM and was hoping for a more exciting and more thought provoking movie. Attack of the Clones delivers BIG!!! From the Jedi counsels involvement with the creation and use of the clone army to the origins of Boba Fett. This story is worthy of the Star Wars name and should rank at the top of the best Star Wars movie along with Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi.

That being said, and before I go into my small list of problems I had with the movie, just let me say I am a Star Wars FANATIC, not just a fan. And before the flames start flying just let me say Episode II is a must see regardless of the few small flaws.

But flaws there are.

1) Hayden Christensen is the worst actor is any of the SW films so far. I am sorry but I didn't believe for a minute that he was going to be the most powerful Jedi in the galaxy. He didn't convince me he was mad when he was supposed to be mad and he didn't seem sad when he was trying to be sad. And if those are the best pickup lines he could come up with, how in the world did he get Padme to fall in love with him. Sorry Hayden but maybe you should go back to acting school.

2) There is no sexual tension between Padme and Anakin. In the book the tension was bursting. But again Hayden and Natalie just didn't pull it off. And why did they make Natalie look like a fruit cake for the first half of the movie and then tried to make her a sex symbol in the second half. Natalie is a Beautiful girl when she is allowed to be, but her nearly see through skintight white outfit was a bit much. And what was up with her hair?

3) My biggest complaint, C3P0 sucks. Sorry all you 3P0 fans but what a crock. Shooting Jedi and, didn't 3P0 get blown apart in ROTJ? And he couldn't talk, not this time, he keeps jabbering on even after two beheadings!! And his annoying voice (was that Anthony Daniels? I don't think so) and forced humor just dragged.

There are some more problems but these are the worst.

And then ALL is redeemed when Yoda and Count Dooko have a battle of the force and then the lightsaber battle to end all lightsaber battles!!! If it weren't for the wounded Kenobi and Skywalker (who Yoda saves twice in 5 minutes) Yoda would have kicked some major Dark Sith Lord butt.

Good Job George, can't wait for Episode III!!!!

title: If you did not like Episode 1, you won't like this.
review:
I'm tremednously disappointed. The chrome wrapped spaceships, all the grassy locations, the high contrast scenes made SW2 a fairy tale. I was saying "Oh my god, am i watching a Backstreet Boys like guy on screen making a very weak love story?"

It's a shame to call THIS plot a SW plot. I'm a very big fan of the 4-5-6 episodes, but I stood up during the endsequence of Episode 1, and I did it again during episode 2's Wedding sequence. I'd recommend everyone to stay away, but everyone will go and see it. Someone may like it. Star Wars will never be the same again. So sad. (The CGI scenes were jerky too, especially when a human character was riding on them.)

There will be thousands of better reviews than this, but I gave almost the first vote here.

3/10 (Ep 1 3/10 also)

Go, and see for yourself. I hope you'll find YOUR Star Wars in it. I could not. :(

title: YODA kicks ass!!!!
review:
Episode II is so much better than Phantom Menace, at least to me. Some say that first par of the movie is boring, I wouldn't say boring, I would say, that some scenes should be shorter and, me personally would change just one completely ( I'm not saying which one), but everything that is shown had to happen and is made far better than Episode I! Attack of the clones has a lot more action and adventure, and just... well, it's great! And of course, YODA IS THE GREATEST LIGHTSABER MASTER EVER!!! In the end ,I would say that Episode II is Great in the beginning-good in the middle- AND THE BEST MOVIE EVER MADE IN THE END!!!! (you'll see because of what)

May the FORCE be with you!!!

title: Keep trying, George
review:
I cannot say this was better than Episode I. If you like space battles, the one at the end of Episode I is better than anything here. If you like lightsaber battles, the one between Qui-Gon Jinn, Obi-wan Kenobi, and Darth Maul in Episode one is more intense and spirited than anything here (Yoda's duel is impressive, no doubt, but lasts nowhere near as long as it should). It is interesting to see a lot of Jedi wielding their lightsabers in combat...but they only chop down those pathetic-looking battle droids. Ho-hum.

If you like good dialogue...there is much more in this film that will make you cringe. Some of the dialogue--especially between Anakin and Padme--is downright embarrassing. If you like computer-generated effects, yes, there is plenty here...but it sometimes looks fake (I think it's because the lighting on the actors often does not match that of the computer-generated backgrounds well).

All is not lost: Christensen is convincing as the troubled young Jedi, and Christopher Lee makes a very smooth villain (although his character seems to come out of nowhere). The story is somewhat more involving, but it's still hard to get interested in the problems of the Republic.

I give this a 7/10. For a really good Star Wars experience, I still recommend the original trilogy.

title: How do you spend millions of dollars and end up with this?
review:
George Lucas has proven that money and fame have taken away from his ability to tell stories. What went wrong? Well let's take a look at this bland, dull, and heartless movie:

Acting? What's acting? You know there's a problem when the best acting in a film comes from the computer generated Yoda. Hey Lucas, you have the talent, we know that they can act, how did they end up looking like actors in a high school play?

Writing? Oh, yeah sure like writings important when you have all kinds of neat computer graphics to look at. Who needs to develop things like dialogue? Really what the point? We have millions of dollars to blow - lets go film a couple of shots in Italy! God knows that with all the CG work on this movie it matters were they film.

Details? Okay, I am starting to get picky here, I know, but come on this stuff gets in the way of good story telling. Here is my short list of details that suck:

  • What's up with the '50s dinner in the middle of Curasant? Give me a break. I am sure - just like here on Earth - that a giant Alien short-order cook is the best resource to investigate a crime.


  • Senator what ever her name, packs her own luggage! This girl has people risk their life's for her, yet she packs her luggage. Here is a government official who knows her place.


  • If I am in charge of building a massive army and some guy wearing a Jedi uniform walks up to me, am I going to take him on a grand tour of our secret Clone Army and tell him all of our strategies? Well yes of course I would.


  • Okay, I am building this super big army of droids on this crazy planet in the middle of nowhere. No doubt that I am using some of the best military technology of the time, but still I fail to notice a massive invasion force of Jedi's and Clones. I think we have an Intel problem. Sure, the Count and the future Emperor planned it that way, but no one else seems to question the ease and surprise of the invasion. Something's wrong here people!


But the details are not the major issue. The issue is that Joseph Campbell is turning in his grave. The original films had the same problems with detail, but they had something that brought the movie to a level above the petty details, they had a story, a human story. This one, as with Episode I, does not. No matter, I'll still go see the next one on opening night.

title: The Best Since Empire... Seriously.
review:
Man, i just don't get how these critics can bash this movie...

I went into the movie theatre at 12:01 AM on Thursday, May 16, expecting the absolute worst. I nearly lost all respect I had for George Lucas after the disaster that was Episode I.

Man, was I blown away.

This plot is THE darkest movie of the Star Wars series (Although I'm sure Episode III will be much darker), and it really shows. The ad campaign at first is very misleading (At least to me), with it appearing to be this happy-go-lucky movie that we're all used to in most summer movies, in which some baddie ends up getting killed in the end, a personal sacrifice to one of the heroes, etc, etc. Not to mention the extreme possibility for a sequel.

But man, does it work here.

The movie's basically an evolution of the character Anakin Skywalker, in which he is slowly beginning to hone his Jedi skills. One of the clever devices used in the movie is the amount of foreshadowing and allusions that are in the movie, ESPECIALLY in the soundtrack. I could actually feel the Dark Side of the Force slowly getting the better of Anakin in the more powerful scenes, which will remain untold due to spoilers, but I'm sure you'll be able to pick them out. Also, it was actually executed pretty well. For instance, a scene with Obi-Wan Kenobi making this statement to something of this effect:

"You're going to be the death of me, Anakin."

Is this Jedi instincts, or what?

Also, there's the love story. I personally didn't think that it worked in the first half or so of the movie, with some of the lines being pure and utter camp. It was hard NOT to laugh at some of the lines of dialogue in the movie. But in the second half of the movie when they enter the climatic battle, man, did it work. The passion the two characters shared actually seemed real.

Plus, who can forget Jango Fett: The Biggest Badass on the Face of the Earth. It was awesome to actually see how he developed this clone army, and you'll certainly be surprised when you find out how his offspring came into place...

If you have any doubts to this movie, then put them away and go see the movie. Ignore the critics, because this is the best movie of 2002 (So far, anyway).

Oh yeah, and Yoda fights with a lightsaber. One of the coolest scenes EVER. PERIOD. =)

title: Didn't take itself too seriously
review:
I anticipated this movie to be good. Unfortunately I did the same thing for Phantom Menace. I was not let down in this case. Although the title leaves something to be desired, the storyline was fairly well done. Acting (Besides Hayden) was incredibly good (As always). In a sense, Hayden did a good job to create dual personas, which obviously will come into play in the next episode.

Besides that beef, Lucas kept Jar Jar at a minimum and that helped GREATLY!!! Costumes were wonderful, effects were awesome. Fight scenes were good, but I felt that Lucas hid some of the fighting with low light and head-shots. But heck, he is the genius movie-maker. Not me.

Overall I cannot wait to see it again. It will be good to see Ep.1 and 2 in a row so my faith in the series will be upheld. And I really can't wait for Episode III!!! I highly suggest seeing this film.

title: Great film, Awesome experience, dialog so-so
review: This is the best in the series so far in my opinion. George Lucas seems to have learned from the mistakes he made in Episode I and more than makes up for them in this movie. Everything is better, the characters, the action, the emotions, the plot development. The only problem I had with the movie was the dialog. It all seems so predictable and cliche, and mostly referencing to other movies. Sure, it's funny when Obi-Wan says "Anakin, you'll be the death of me someday", but it reminded me more of the Jay and Silent Bob movie with all those clever little quips. Of course, I still gave it a 10, because it is so perfectly done in every other aspect.

title: Disappointment
review:
I've been waiting for this installment, hoping it would be better than the last one. I saw an early review that was very positive and got excited about it based on that.

Hype, hype and more standard Star Wars hype. I was not impressed with the movie. Like the last one the sequence of actions did not flow smoothly. Many scenes where the characters did incredibly stupid things that just did not seem "real". They cut down Jar-Jar binks, but replaced his annoying chatter with way too much C3PO.

Other than a few good scenes, I was overall very disappointed with the movie.

title: A Visually Exhausting film that takes a step in the right direction...
review:
Star Wars Episode II: Attack of the Clones' can best be described as a transitional film in which we are right in the middle of the ultimate conversion from good to evil. Hayden Christensen is not miscast as the hormone infused Anakin Skywalker who treads on love with Senator Padme Amidala (Natalie Portman). Episode II' seems to improve upon the needed improvements that were so pervasive in Episode I'. That being said, it still has its' flaws. Director George Lucas embeds his film with digital imagery that exhausts the viewer. I have comes to term with this trait that I only experience when watching these Star Wars' films (Episode I & 2) and have keenly labeled the concept Visual Exhaustion'. This is because Lucas puts 95% of the film through a digital filter. To some this can be an alluring trait, but in my personal opinion it seems as if he has come to rely wholeheartedly on digital imagery to convey a story. This was the severe case that we encountered upon Episode I. The hype surrounding that film was maniacal and had many people; including myself, disappointed with the first foray into the Galactic Tale that we had so eagerly awaited. Yet, in Episode II, we see Lucas actually focusing on telling a story and although the story might not as be as interesting as the later chapters are (Episode 4, 5, 6) we still are captivated by the young Hayden Christensen. This virtually unknown actor inhibits several characteristics that will lead into the third part which I will be anxiously awaiting. I must admit, I was severely turned off by Episode I' and wanted to loathe this film, but Lucas seems to have revamped the franchise and has focused on telling a story and not selling toys. Good move George, you have partially restored some integrity back into the franchise. Improvements are seen in the overall design of the film. The plot involves some more origins being uncovered as an assassination attempt on Senator Amidala leads to a civil war in the galaxy as Count Dooku (Christopher Lee) attempts at destroying the Galaxy through a separatist movement. This in turn forces the Senate to develop an army in order to ensure safety as there are not enough Jedi for thorough protection. The clones in question are the Storm Troopers we see in future films under the Direct Command of Lord Vader. Confused yet? You should be. I always thought Lucas complicated his scripts by tackling too much content as back story and there is no difference here. Trade Wars, Colonies and Separatists are all part of this plot that leads into one pivotal event  the conversion of young Skywalker to the dark side. What I found interesting was the manner in which the film cleverly foreshadowed the events to come surrounding young Skywalker. Perhaps foreshadowing is not the best word to use since we all know of Skywalker's fate, but during the film we see clever scenarios that display the innate rage, madness and anger this young Jedi possesses. Skywalker's progress as a young man is a crucial element in this film as we are exposed to his much darker side that really spotlights him as a trouble-maker. Skywalker is slowly becoming disenchanted with the Rules a Jedi must follow and finds himself falling out of favor with his Masters. This in turn leads to a slow, yet gradual progression towards the Dark Side. It must be noted that Episode II is far superior to Episode I. As aforementioned, it does have its' flaws specifically in terms of dialogue. Yet it is also clear that Lucas had the script somewhat doctored for cohesiveness; something that was missing in Episode I. Writer Jonathan Hales (The Scorpion King) was called upon to clear some points but the dialogue still suffers as we are in for some of the weakest romantic dialogue in a long time. The interplay between Skywalker and Amidala is gushing with uncomforting romance as these two characters plot out their love and their lives. Lucas opens the film with a great action sequence involving the pursuit of an assassin which is extremely entertaining. The sets in the introductory sequence seem to be lifted from Spielberg's A.I.' as the dizzying lights and glamour of a Galactic city come to life. This interesting action sequence seemingly sets the tone for what is a visually exhausting yet solid attempt at getting the franchise in the direction which it should be headed. Lucas uses the same transitional progression as he did with the later chapters in terms of pace and character development. Episode II' serves to hopefully build towards a cataclysmic and dark third piece that resolves all. Yet, the stereotypical Alien characters are back in full force and the pounding score from musical genius John Williams accompanies this tale that is a step ahead from Episode I, but a few steps back from the magic that was Star Wars'.

Giancarlo's Rating: **

title: Great Movie
review: This movie is great and is full of action. It is great for a Star Wars buff and for just normal people. All of the boringness in The Phantom Menace opened up every thing. Most of the middle of the movie was based on Anakin and Senator Amidala being in love which was just down right retarded. But otherwise a great action Star Wars movie!!!!!!!

title: Star Wars is Back!
review: I've said a lot of bad stuff about George Lucas since The Phantom Menace was released.  I, like a lot of other fans, thought that he was intentionally trying to ruin the Star Wars saga.  Well, I still stand by all the negative stuff I've said about Phantom Menace, but Lucas has redeemed himself.  Attack of the Clones is awesome. Count Dooku is great, and Jango Fett rules!  I was really worried about seeing Boba Fett as a young boy, worried that it might be Jake LLoyd all over again, but little Boba is really cool.  Restrained, alert, and utterly devoted to his father, we see in his father what he will one day become.  Go see this movie! It is worthy to bear the name Star Wars!

title: Yoda Fighting - Greatest moments in cinema history
review: As a rather avid star wars fan, it seems blasphemous to give the newest addition of the series such love, but I can't however, find flaw with Episode 2.  It is a non-stop rollercoaster ride, with enough light saber action to satisfy the most discerning of critics, and a romantic sub-plot that is both entertaining and moving.  George Lucas really does himself rather proud, and Yoda fighting...well.

title: childhood fantasies redone
review:
Some friends and I were waiting 2 hours in line last night to show our support for struggling film company Lucasfilm's latest amalgamation of collective conciousness's hopes and dreams entitled Attic of the Clowns. In line I wondered what people would think of the series thirty years from now. What my children would think of it. (Though waiting in line for Star Wars movies will likely not add to my procreating anytime soon.)

I couldn't help but breathe deep in an effort to calm my fluttering heart. So many years of boredom would hopefully be soothed in the two hours, thirteen minutes. I would soon enjoy utter and complete Star Wars release.

People complain that they know what's going to happen and therefore these prequels are tarnished. But one must not look a these films, or any film, or anything that can purport to being art, from that perspective. If twenty years from now I'm sitting with my children watching all six films in a row, (which I guess Lucas was going for as opposed to us watching the last three then the first three) that won't be the point. And if the films are held up as touchstones for generations--which in our culturally barren and getting more so each day world, that could very well be possible--they're not going to care what order they come out in. actually, I saw Jedi first (at age four in the theatre), then Star Wars, then Empire, then Phantom Menace. And I imagine that the love scenes I see passing between Portman and Christensen will still make me green with envy as they are living in a world where actions matter, and I'm worrying about bills and what to say to my wife to bring the love back to our marriage. That's all beside the point, as viewing the movie changed all my rhythms of existence and experience of time, as films should.

People also complain about the love story element of this movie, but that's because they're comparing it with films, stories, and plays of our time--of works they're comfortable with--and here I think that Lucas's love story's sterility and alienness actually further the believability of the piece. True, some of the dialog seems generated on a BASIC program, but the complete otherness of their love forced me into a place where I believed they were existing in a world where the rules we understand and take for granted simply don't apply. Perhaps it would have been best if they did not speak at all.

In fact, it reminded me of what love was like before the hyperkinetic notions of romance we understand as the-only-way-to-love-today existed. In medieval European times (on which the pacing of these films are based) courtship was fast, often silent, and loved ones didn't speak. They had no need to. They weren't trained to exist by television and scripted fabrications and patterns of existence.

Compare the love scenes in this to those in Kubrick's Barry Lydon for a different AOTC romance comparison than, say, to "Dawson's Creek." They love in a totally different fashion and as far as I'm concerned, the more difficult to understand, the further our regular lives are placed from the Star Wars universe and the more believable it becomes. The characters and events should not operate on the same grounds that we do. And for the most part, they don't. I even found myself wondering, "do these people have sex in the same way we do?" "Do they even do that?" and such questioning of these basic principles and assumptions great art do make.

As for the climactic battle sequence, the attack of the clones, I thoroughly enjoyed it. The points of the film that did relate the Star Wars universe to ours brought it down a notch for me. If these people are so technologically advanced, why would they still be fighting ground wars? The last ten years of military exercises on the part of America seemed more technologically advanced than most or all of the Clones stuff and a single bomber in our Great American Arsenal could have rendered the great clone army and the great robot army moot. And why would Jedis risk their lives fighting robots on a ground war when 1990 United States War Machine could take out an Iraqi soldier from 5 miles up?(By the way, good referencing the Vietnam helicopter infantry in that finale scene, Lucas) If Jedi's have the technological wherewithal to fold space, why can't they accomplish similar things? One can't delve into such scientific minutia in certain parts of the film (e.g. explanations and displays of cloning) and not elsewhere. To make this all work, we have to be experiencing the movie as not relating to our understanding of physics at all, but that they evolved differently and perhaps were unable to perform such military actions, unable to feel and express such Earthling affection. They still fight in medieval fashion. There aren't even any trenches here, they must love in such an alternate manner as well. Perhaps that the only way these people are built. Who knows, accept their reality for what it is and enjoy the film. I certainly did.

title: Yoda stole the show . . .
review:
For me only one thing stands out so memorable from Star Wars Episode II Attack of The Clones is that green muppet fighting with a lightsaber with the full force as his ally in the final lightsaber battle sequence of the film. Yes this is what blew me away! The chase was magnificent, love story was average, the massive battles were excellent but it was the little Green Jedi who is the Jedi of all Jedi who at times sounds like Grover who stole the show. It might have been five minutes his whole fight scene but it was the sweetest five minutes of cinema for one moviegoer in their life. I believe Mr Lucas should redesign the Attack of The Clones movie poster and just put Yoda on there in his karate stance. For me the movie now just has Yoda written all over it. When the 2003 Oscars come the Academy should make a break on the usual traditions and award Yoda for his action performance. This would be one moment I would love to see happen in my life. Yoda deserves it and it should really be his second Oscar after his excellent performance in Empire. So let the Oscar Hype begin for Yoda for the best performance as the leading actor in a motion picture.

Besides Yoda, the movie has redeemed Lucas I believe. It is much better than Episode 1. It was a great story (just the love story part got very average, made Anakin seem too much of a stalker at times I thought) that gets you going right to the end and makes you wish Episode III comes out very soon. The dialogue was good especially the 'Death Sticks' part but then got flat a few times. The characters were great especially Palpatine/Sidious and Dooku but I wish that Mace and Jango had more time on screen to strut more of their amazing skill. Another surprise I thought was that Jar Jar seemed funny for once especially when he greets Obi-Wan after so many years. The acting was great and Mr Christensen passes with flying colours as Anakin. The special effects were out of this world and same for the action too. I recommend this to Star Wars fan or not to see. I rate this 9 out of 10 and out of the Star Wars movies I would rate AOTC in the following. Empire, A New Hope, AOTC, Jedi and finally Phantom.

title: Amazing!
review:
I got a chance to see Episode II last night, and let me tell you, I wasn't disappointed. I would see things that were absent in the Phantom Menace, for example, the presence of humour, and the storyline that we all remember from the original Trilogy. Does this film compare to any of the old films? No, it doesn't.

There is only one part that I am opposed to, and that was the quality of the love scenes. I believe that the love scenes contained one cliche after another, and all the usual lines from all other cliched romance movies, however we must understand that Mr. Lucas had to put them in there, because if he didn't, Luke and Leia wouldn't have been around in Episodes 4, 5, and 6. In consideration to the negative aspect, we must understand that there was one for every film. We hated C-3PO in the Empire Strikes Back, the Ewoks in Return of the Jedi, and Jar Jar in the Phantom Menace.

The reason why I loved this film came up, and no one can say that it wasn't relevant. Personally, I enjoyed the sequences after the Romance, especially one involving a character we all know and love. The battles scenes were intense and graphic for a PG film, but like I just said, they were intense. These scenes certainly opened the door to not just Episode 3, but Episode 4 as well. It entertained us, and kept us in perpetual suspense, considering we have an idea as to what happens next.

In conclusion, the storyline was good, the romance was bad, and the battle scenes compensated for it. I am looking forward for 2005, when we will kiss Star Wars good-bye. I recommend this film to anyone who likes Film War, or Star Wars.

title: Attack of the "effects"?
review:
Starting with the highlights: Absolutely superb effects all through the movie! My favourite was Yoda's light sabre duel. The depth & detail of the scenes was almost unbelievable it was so realistic. This film was a definite improvement on Episode 1.

A bit on the negative: Too much romance! In the words of my son: "It was Star Wars for women." Anakin & Amidala gave fine performances; But we don't go to a Star Wars movie for love scenes. (At least he didn't say "yippee" this time.)

The ending sort of left you hanging. But then so did The Empire Strikes Back. This is not necessarily a bad thing; but unlike "Empire Strikes Back" it seemed there should be a bit more wrap up.

I didn't notice anything spectacular about the acting. But the major actors carried their roles well (as usual). The new Anakin did much better than I expected.

All in all, I really liked the movie. It had all the requirements for the classic Star Wars movie: Plenty of action, lots of impressive effects, fantastic scenes (the best ever) and more exotic characters....And Jar Jar wasn't a major presence to my great relief.

title: Worse than Episode 1
review: This one is even worse than Episode 1. Instead of JarJar annoying us now we have a silly lovestory and a dying mother. The only good things about this movie was to see Yoda himself fighting with a lightsaber. The acting of Christopher Lee was very good as always. But in general the movie was very disappointing, it is definately not as good as any of the original Star Wars movies. I rate it 5/10.

title: Possibly the best in the trilogy!
review: Imagine this was a non-star wars movie... just imagine that. It would have rave reviews, most critics would praise it... but for some reason "star wars" is already held higher than other movies. people expect too much these days. if you (re)watch the original trilogy, especially a new hope, you will find a lot of poor dialogue, plot flaws and certainly bad acting. this movie was extremely well done. the acting was superb. ewan mcgregor mimicks alec guiness to the key! Hayden Christensen is a good desgruntled anakin. i have seen other movies with him, and it seems this is the role he hits right on the nose. natalie portman was not only extremely sexy but developed as a character. instead of being the monotonous character from episode 1, she is a fun loving, emotional beauty. christopher lee plays both sides perfectly, but Ian McDiarmid does it even better. the visuals in this movie blow away spiderman, the matrix and any other "blockbuster" movies to be released. it easily blows away films unworthy of the best visual effects award. it even rivals the lord of the rings. the dialogue between the two lovers is exactly how most young adults act and talk. yes it is cheesy at times, but isn't that the way all young lovers are? the plot was *brilliant*. the jango fett/bobba fett relationship was ingenius. watching obi-wan on his investigation was fascinating. jar jar was *not* annoying at all. c3po and r2d2 almost stole the show, but the real person who stole it (and who will be remembered for it) is yoda! nothing, not even gandalf vs the balrog, can compare to yoda fighting. i was in pure ecstatic bliss and awe. is it better than episode one? hells ya! easily! better than jedi? for sure. better than the original? in my opinion yes. better than empire? it's a tough call, but considering that lucas had very little to work with since he *had* to get in many subplots to fill in episodes 4-6 (which, btw, worked perfectly, ie. lars owen) it definetely can rival it. there are *sooo* many parallels to episode 5 (empire) that are just wonderous to watch, and the cliffhanger finalé really makes me want a lot more. only 3 more years of waiting until the circle is complete. lucas has truly made a masterpiece. ps, i can't wait to see it on pure digital screen!

title: Bring some earplugs!
review:
Fool me once, shame on you. Fool me twice, shame on me!

I was absolutely certain that Mr. Lucas had learned from his Episode 1 mistakes and would be packaging a wonderful treat for us this go 'round. Well, it's true that he fixed many of the annoying problems that plagued us die-hard fans in episode 1. Instead we have a whole new set of problems that make much of this film very difficult to watch, indeed. Some of the lines the poor actors have to deliver you can hardly believe are coming from their mouths. You can tell by the expressions on their faces that they are having a hard time with it also.

The human element that made Episodes IV-VI so much fun to watch is almost completely gone. It is quite apparent that George knows and cares a heck of a lot more about special effects/technical wizardry than he does about script, plot, and characters that you really care about, good or bad. I wonder if it ever occurred to him that one of the reasons that the first three movies were so popular were because he was limited with what he could do with effects and so he HAD to focus on the characters to make the movie worth watching.

Oh well, with all that said, there's plenty of neat things to watch in this movie. I would put it up on the same level as many of the Blue Angels IMAX films I've seen recently. Just replace the horrible script and dialogue with some Tom Selleck narration, and you might just have a movie that doesn't make you cringe every time the actors open their mouths.

Shame on me this time!

Ian

--

"Who is more foolish, the fool, or the fool who follows him?"

title: Seeing it at midnight with die-hard fans is the only way to go
review:
While it is a bit slow in the first 1/3, and the acting is (like all of them) pretty much terrible across the board, the last 2/3 of the movie do split into 2 separate story lines that are interesting and do hold your attention...

That is when Star Wars is the most fun, when it follows, and bounces, between several different plots...

title: Uninspired
review:
Uninspired acting. Slow plot. See it, but only once.

I don't know if it was dry acting or that was the best that could be done with such lines. I thought the effects where cool, but very overdone. Fancy effects and robust background activity can't cover a poor, tired, old story.

title: This is it!
review:
have to say, I was completely blown away...this totally blew Episode I out of the water within ten minutes, and, frankly, it rivals Return of the Jedi. The audience clapped as soon as the Fox logo came on, roared with cheers when the Lucasfilm logo came on, and, well, all hell broke loose when the words "A long time ago in a galaxy far, far away...." came on the screen. Pure delight.

As far as the film...the best summary was what the CNN critic said: "It's dark but has wonderfully funny moments; you care about the characters; and the action and special effects are first-rate." The fight sequences, especially the final one, were amazingly intense. Lucas' directing during the lightsaber battle made beautiful use of colors, shadows, and intensity. There was also some very witty dialogue; I was particularly happy to see the C-3PO/R2-D2 banter back in full force.

Yes, some of the romantic dialogue was stilted, but I actually found most to be fine...aside from a "Sound of Music"-like moment, it was played out nicely. I was also surprised by how dark some sequences were, and how intense it was. But on the subject of reactions, if this taught me anything, it was that a lot of critics "just don't get it." They don't like the movie? Screw them. It was great. I'm not saying that because I was a fan. Two definite non-fans were with me, and they loved it. I'm saying it because it was everything I wanted it to be, and more.

But really, I was impressed with the characters...given the negativity I heard about Natalie Portman, I thought she was fine overall. I thought Hayden Christensen was great (I have to confess that I and everyone else who think he's hot, which seems to be everyone, appreciated what appeared to be a shot that George Lucas filmed to give a male equivalent of the pure eroticism of the Princess Leia metal slave bikini, LOL). Ewan McGregor was, as always, great, but it was Samuel L. Jackson, Christopher Lee, and Temuera Morrison who stole the show.

Wait, no. They almost stole it. It was Yoda who stole the show. The final confrontation...well...now we know why Yoda is the master. :o) The audience was literally on their feet, cheering and screaming with joy. It was incredible.

When the lights came up, just about everyone was screaming and cheering and overjoyed...definitely a great sight to see, since The Phantom Menace left a sour taste in so many people's mouths.

I loved it. Loved it loved it loved it loved it, and I can't wait to see it again tomorrow. Thank you, George Lucas. We love you.

title: Better, but not great
review: Much better than the Phantom Menace, but still could have been better.  A little slow in the middle, but a solid 7 none-the-less.  I saw it at 12:15 am on the 16th and at some points I struggled to stay awake (my girlfriend fell asleep after the first 45 minutes).  Great ending, but the rest was decent at best.

title: Great Story...Poorly Told
review: The entire Star Wars saga is a fantastical and brilliantly imaginative concept, but, ironically, in the hands of its creator, the story is done a great injustice.  Unlike Episodes IV,V and VI, which benefited from both simplicity (Lucas couldn't go overboard in A New Hope) and outside influence (different directors amongst other input in V & VI), Episode II is beleaguered by Lucas's autocratic control of his creation. Plainly, Lucas is a bad storyteller. In Episode II, all the elements that made the first three films classics are there: the strong, and interconnecting themes of good and evil, the inventiveness  and most definitely the effects.  However, the merits of these elements are largely lost in Lucas's inability to use the power of images and the techniques of film to tell his tale.  He insults the audience by relying on unnecessary exposition, worsened by elementary dialogue, to carry his plot points, rather than letting a telling glance or a shadowy sneer do the work for him (e.g. Ankin/Amidala scene by fire or before they enter the coliseum, etc.).  This compounded with flat direction and poor editing, create an unbalanced film lacking in emotion. Unfortunately, when you get down to brass tacks, there are some outstanding scenes and imagery in this film that if reworked could have yielded a much more effective product.  I love Star Wars, and will probably give this film more credit than it deserves, as it helps close another chapter of a story that I feel so connected with, but I can't help but think that if this weren't part of the "Saga" I'd be p***ed I spent my 10 bucks to go see it.

title: George........less can be more sometimes
review:
Where to start with Attack of the Clones. After the heartbreaking disappointment of The Phantom Menace ("yippee","mesa Jar-Jar") - and having watched it several times, it is still a disappointment - my expectations were lower for this one. But over the last few days before it's release, I started to get excited again.

SPOILER ALERT - DO NOT READ UNTIL SEEN MOVIE

Sitting in the theatre, the music starts and Star Wars appears..the stomach butterflies start fluttering. As the movie gets going, I jump from feeling excited and remember the thrill of seeing A New Hope when I was 6 to cringing at the extra-clunky dialogue and laughing at the hopeless emoting of Hayden Christensen, especially with Natalie Portman's Senator. And the less said about the death of Anakin's mother, the better.........let's just say that everyone in the audience was laughing out loud. What happened to the George Lucas of American Graffitti and the original trilogy? I think that he has spent too much time playing with his CGI-toolbox - almost everything has a false sheen to it........we even see Anakin and Padme eat CGI fruit!!! Every scene has to have some creature lurking at some corner of the frame.

But there are good things..............for one, it is better than the Phantom Menace. Much better. There is less Jar-Jar - only this time C3P0 takes his place as the annoying character. The action is exciting, sweeping and, at times, breathtaking. Ewan, Sam and Christopher Lee take the acting kudos; Ewan especially is growing into Alec Guinness in A New Hope. By far the best section of the movie is the latter part when George gets the multiple action scenes going, and who would have expected Yoda to prove what you only hear about as concerns his Jedi powers - this got everyone cheering and clapping. Lucas is also readying, a la Empire Strikes Back, the movie audience for a stunning 3rd instalment.

So, to sum up, Lucas is getting there but the soul of the series is in danger of being overwhelmed by the reliance on CGI. Oh, to be 6 years old again.

title: A movie rush for two+half hours!
review:
Being in my early 30's, which means that I grew with the Original Trilogy, I am one of those people that were genuinely interested to know, in the Star Wars storyline, what happened before the Original Trilogy, and after. Timothy Zahn's books were great, and covered most of the Trilogy future; so when George Lucas announced he will be filming the first Trilogy, and changed the focus from Luke Skywalker to make it a six-part story on Anakin Skywalker/Darth Vader, my interest grew more.

"The Phantom Menace", as a *story* unwrapped in the past, was something I found clever and good. Anakin, as a boy slave, is found and taken to the Jedi Council for training. We get to know Amidala, who will later become the mother of the Skywalkers we met in the Original Trilogy. Clever story; but the film itself, disappointed me more than expected. When I read that Lucas was mainly addressing TPM to youngsters, I accepted it--besides, it's his own work and life dream, and I cannot judge that.

Following TPM and the internet fuss (including the notorious "Phantom Edit", an edited version of TPM) I believe Lucas got the message; he has to do a more serious storytelling, and not forget that the majority of fans are adults, living up to the expectation to see something spectacular in terms of story and visuals. And I think he achieved this, with Attack Of The Clones, a title that many disliked but was necessary, to my point of view, to set the pace for things to come.

The film itself is a feast for the eyes--George Lucas overdid it this time, and the ILM guys probably got PhDs in special effects. Although the dialogues needed more 'polishing', the film itself adds a new tone and becomes a vital part in the Star Wars storyline.

When I saw the film in a journalist premiere on my birthday! here in Athens, Greece, I felt again the same excitement when the STAR WARS logo opened the film. I wanted Lucas to heal the TPM disappointment, and he did. I left the theatre (DTS ES 6.1 sounds great) and still felt the adrenaline pumping. I was pleased, and it's not something that every film does to me.

I read reports before and after seeing "Attack Of The Clones" and in most part, people have some 'logical' reasons to be disappointed again by the thinner story, the not-so worked dialogues and the extended scenes on the love between Anakin and Padme/Amidala. But I am willing to accept that. Why?

First of all, one cannot compare the Original Trilogy to the current. Different style, Hollywood has itself changed a lot since the late 70's.

Secondly, Lucas said that the effects he is exhibiting have always been the effects he wanted on the Original Trilogy--so it's not really a question "do the effects make the film or the film needs the effects"? A counter-balance to that was The Matrix, where the effects served the film, did not make the film.

Finally, accept this film as ENTERTAINMENT, not as the story of your life. Do not go to see it with high and serious expectations--just 'free your mind'. I can classify this more of a "pop-corn movie" than serious viewing; I remember the same happened with Independence Day. People did not like it initially, me neither. We took it very seriously, but eventually I accepted it as a "pop-corn movie" and enjoyed it--even bought the AC-3 laserdisc and later the Special Edition on DVD...

I know I did not write a lot on the film itself, but "Attack Of The Clones" remains a George Lucas creation. The man has the power to do whatever he wants, however he wants it. We can only accept this, and enjoy the film; it is really up to us. As for myself, I enjoyed it enormously and rated it 7 out of 10.

title: Painful to watch
review:
Putting media hype aside, here are my thoughts on the second Star Wars movie.

I gave this movie a 3 out 10.

The visual effects were great. But visuals alone do not make a movie.

Story line. Well, there was no story, just a series of events. A few pieces fell into place to explain the story in episode 4.

Acting. It was painful to watch Hayden Christensen. The boy can't act. The rest of the cast did alright - but nothing outstanding.

Now for the media hype. I have read in the media, of scenes compared to great movies such as Gladiator and The Matrix

The Gladiator reference is miles off the mark. They were in a stadium and thats about as close as it came to the Gladiator movie.

Associating Yoda with The Matrix is both a joke and an insult. See for yourself and you will understand what I mean.

Overall, the movie was boring. A few people left half way through the movie. I must admit, I was tempted to leave too. There was no excitement, no suspense, no twists and turns.

Slightly better than Phantom, but another poor effort by Lucas.

title: A vast improvement over Episode I!!
review: My family and I just returned from one of the Sunday, May 12th benefit showings of Episode II, and we're glad to say that it really lives up to being a "Star Wars" film.  So much happens story-wise that explains what is to come that I'm not sure one could get it all in just one viewing.  The effects and sound were excellent; we were fortunate enough to view it in a theater that recently installed a digital projector, and the picture and sound are a welcome improvement over actual film.  I don't think "Star Wars" fans will be disappointed in this installment as they likely were with Episode I.  It's not a perfect film, but it was satisfying enough, particularly in its plot lines and their developments.  We already have tickets for opening day, May 16th, and are eagerly awaiting seeing it again to pick up on what we missed.  Overall, not as good as Episodes IV and V, but better than Episode VI, and much, much better than Episode I.

title: LET DOWN!!!
review:
SPOILERS ALERT

When you go see "Attack of the clones" Just take a nap for the first 20 hours of the movie. I went to see this movie at 10 oclock at night on opening night and man lemme tell you it was the biggest let down of the year. The story is great but lucas does not go anywhere with it!!!! Then the next hour of the movie are the jedi counsel talking and Anni and Amidala gettinga little "closer" then just talking. All while Obi won is trying to save the galaxy by himself. !!!!!!!!!
