title: "The Top Ten list"
review:
OK, here are top ten reasons to watch this movie:

#10. The romantic story was genuinely intriguing. It was interesting to see, despite how enraged Anakin got, Amidala still fell for him. He admitted he slaughtered an entire village of sand people, and she comforted him. Even in a galaxy far, far away, love is blind.

#9. No talk of "metichlorines." There was too much of this Scully-esquire approach to explaining the force in "Phantom menace". Good Riddance.

#8. To see Luke's old home. Not just his home world as in Phantom Menace, but his home. Anakin and Amidala sat at the same table as Luke did when he dreamed of exploration with his Uncle and Aunt. It raises questions in the complete story line as a whole. Like, it will be interesting to see in part three why Anakin is unable to figure out his son was brought to this very place to be raised. Anyway, it's fun to see the old set after all these years.

#7. The special effects. I don't care what anybody says, the effects are impressive, most impressive. The scene where Obi-Wan and Anakin chase the assassin was pretty darn amazing.

#6. The characters and the acting was better than "Phantom Menace." But that's not really saying much. Hayden Christenson, not my favorite actor, but a lot less annoying than that young brat in the first movie. The scene that really made me aware of how good these actors were, was in the "gladiator arena" scene played out in true Star Wars fashion of the original trilogy. The three lead characters were chained to over-sized pillars, and what was played out here was very reminiscent of Luke, Leia and Han. No, Portman, Christiansen and Ewan McGregor still don't quite have the same chemistry as Mark Hamill, Carrie Fisher and Harrison Ford, but they came pretty darn close.

#5. To watch more of George Lucas's back story---as fallible, inconsistent and contradictory as it might be (I see at least one other commenter also had a problem with Threepio and Owen Lars living with each other in this story line. Wasn't the fact that Darth Vader built threepio bad enough? Did Lucas forget Owen Lars purchased Threepio years later in "A New Hope"--somebody ought to point that out to him). With that said, this story does have more depth than "The Phantom Menace" or "Return of the Jedi." This installment is simply a stronger piece in the puzzle. Glad to see Lucas still has a magnificent mind, and still knows how to tell a good story.

#4. Much like the second installment in the first trilogy ("Empire Strike's back), this was a darker tale. I liked it!

#3. A lot less Jar-Jar!! I almost forgot he was in the movie at all. THANK YOU, George! and if you cut him out of the script completely in the third one, we really won't miss him...really!

#2. More Threepio and R2. Yeah baby, Lucas knows what we want to see.

#1. Without a doubt the number one reason--by far--this movie was worth watching just to see Yoda's light saber scene! He truly floated like a butterfly and stung like a bee. Absolutely funny, yet so great to see the little guy fight! While I was watching that scene, I remember thinking "this is so great! Yoda RULES!!" I laughed, I cheered! All of us who watched Yoda in earlier films wondered, "how can he be a Jedi? Jedi must defend peace and this must entail being a skilled light sabersman." Now we know, we finally know! Bravo George, Bravo!! But, can someone explain to me how Yoda can move that fast, jump, heck nearly fly in the air, then afterward pick up his walking stick and slowly move about . I'm sure there is a reason, perhaps something to do with the force, but it escapes me.

Now, I won't go as far to say this movie is better than "A New Hope" or "Empire Strikes Back". But, Lucas has learned his lesson from "The Phantom Menace" and made significant improvements. Not quite enough for my taste, but it's still Star Wars. In what other movie can the "story teller" disappoint us, yet we still line up to pay $8.50 to see it. And gladly do it all over again.

title: "TRULY... DEEPLY... DESPICABLE"
review:
Apart from the usual fantastic special effects we are used to seeing from George Lucas, this movie lacks the drama the original trilogy put forth.

These prequels have been one disappointment to the other.

Phantom Menace: I speak for all of us when I say: Jar Jar Binks?

Attack of the Clones: Spare me the corny details of Anakin and Amidala's love affair! We understand they eventually had to fall in love, we knew it all along, so why do we have to see them frolicking around green pastures? Han Solo and Leia were in love and we didn't have to take this torture. As if it isn't bad enough, the dialogues seem to be written by a couple of 8 year olds.

What happened to Obi Wan? Was he this idiotic Jedi who had to wait to be an old geezer to win our hearts and BECOME wise?

Yoda's gift is wisdom, he's not an action figure!

What's up with the assembly line scene? What's that got to do with anything? We know they're making droids! I wish they would stop underestimating us.

Let me get this straight, Jango Fett is a bounty hunter? Why does he hire a "changer" (whatever the hell that is) to do his dirty work? Is it absolutely necessary for Boba Fett to be even in this film?

I could go on forever but...

In a nutshell, Attack of the Clones is better than Phantom Menace but it doesn't stand a chance against the original Star Wars trilogy.

On a positive note: Jar Jar Binks is over and done with!

title: Lucas, Why the HELL did you make Boba Fett SO ANNOYING!?!?!

title: Superb in places, downright laughable in others
review:
I think the general consensus of The Phantom Menace was that it was a fairly enjoyable load of rubbish. Light-hearted nonsense which had a slight comic-book approach. The idea of Attack of the Clones was that it was a touch darker, a bit more brooding. Well, after finally having seen this my verdict was that while the basic story was generally strong, and the special effects absolutely brilliant in places, there were a number of glaring weaknesses which moderately crippled it. The strengths were that it felt far more like Star Wars than the previous effort - the scenery was breathtaking and it encompassed the 'familiar yet alien world' that Star Wars has always used.

The characters were an intriguing bunch: Obi Wan Kenobi, as played by Ewan McGregor, was a far more authoritive presence than in TPM (The Phantom Menace). He commanded a little more respect. McGregor doesn't quite have the air of Alec Guiness, but he's done a lot better here than we might have expected. Anakin Skywalker (Hayden Christensen) has grown up, obviously, and comes across as an arrogant upstart whose self-belief outways him. There are plenty of subtle hints of his impending joining of the Dark Side. He's generically acted, but not badly. Senator PadmÃ© Amidala is far less wooden than she was in TPM, in fact I thought Portman's performance in TPM was positively poor. But she elicits far more empathy and warmth here, and does admirably better. Generally the story is fairly gripping, if perhaps suffering from the same flaws that TPM did, only not so badly. Again, the plot really isn't that great and the viewer find themselves simply going on a ride in the Star Wars world. In many ways, while this is a better movie that TPM, it's structured similarly.

The element that brings it down badly is the unintended humour. There is a love story in here, and it is cringe-worthily badly done. Quite honestly I wonder if indeed the humour wasn't intended, because I found it rather hilarious in places. In fact one part had me almost in tears - I'll say 'waterwall' and you'll agree.

Plus our old chum Joda gets into a light-sabre battle with an enemy, and it is a combination of the coolest thing you ever saw, and the funniest.

Overall, well worth going to see, but I can't help but feel Lucas will never make any of these prequels as well as he did the subsequent 3 back in the 70s and 80s.

title: Flawed, but still great entertainment
review:
The arrival of a new Star Wars film always prompts expectations of

the perfect action adventure epic, with state of the art effects, all

crammed into 120 minutes. Somehow people always seem to forget that the

original films consisted of little more than great action sequences strung

together with absurd dialogue, perfunctory acting and tenuous plots.

However the fact that everyone is getting hot and bothered over the fifth installment

shows that not even a conscious effort to derail the series, as Jar Jar

Binks surely must have been, can stop this behemoth now.

Attack Of The Clones opens with Obi Wan Kenobi and trainee Jedi

Anakin Skywalker being assigned to protect Senator Padme Amedala,

and soon finds the master chasing across the galaxy to find an assassin whilst

the apprentice struggles with his feelings for the senator. Fitted in

amongst the scenes which show the rise of the evil empire are the usual

assortment of light-sabre fights and space-craft duels.

The film has a darkness to it that few other family films posses.

There is genuine torture and pain shown on screen, possibly as a

reaction to the inanities of The Phantom Menace. Unfortunately this darkness,

typified by Hayden Christensen's broodingly wooden performance as the

future Darth Vader (think of a big gnarly tree on a dark stormy night), seems to

come at the expense of the charisma that characters such as Han Solo

and Princess Leia exuded.

This is compounded by a wayward middle section where the film

threatens to grind to a halt. The scenes of Padme and Anakin picnicking in

grassy mountains looks worryingly like a homage to The Sound Of Music,

whilst Obi-Wan's attempts to become an intergalactic Philip Marlowe are

as pedestrian as a zebra crossing, with Ewan Macgregor's most

mature performance to date being frustrated by having hold his

conversations with an incomprehensible up-turned dustbin. The dialogue of the

original films may have been clunky but at least it was distinctive and delivered

with panache, here the only memorable lines are in-jokes about the

later films.

The film is stolen by an old hand in new clothes. Yoda, now freed

from the indignities of having Frank Oz's hand up his backside, thanks to

some of the most remarkable CGI ever seen, rejoices in being able to wander

freely into battle. His jumbled up dialogue is as eccentric and enjoyable as

ever. However Yoda's greatest moment in the film comes when he

finally draws a lightsaber and engages in battle, a scene which will be played out

to the sound of the jaws of entire audiences hitting the floor in unison the

world over. The fact that a 3 front tall old-codger can convincing be

portrayed as the most powerful warrior in the universe is testament to the power

of Lucas' fantasy worlds, and it is here that the viewer is reminded

why Star Wars became so successful.

The general character and plot limitations are not as bad as

Titanic or Pearl Harbour (though you'll feel only a concerted effort could

produce scripts that inept) and the effects are superior to both. The opening

scenes, based in a over-crowded metropolis are highly reminiscent of Ridley Scott's Blade Runner and have a depth and richness to them that

out-does most real location shooting. However whilst the set-pieces are

well constructed throughout, some of them seem like they were

designed as Playstation games, a feeling which the computer generated effects

only reinforce.

These quibbles are all forgotten in a finale which withstands

comparison with anything committed to film (or high definition digital video).

More than anything the appeal of the Star Wars films lies in their

celebration to the classic swashbuckling films of Errol Flynn and the Zorro

serials and the last 20 minutes serves up giant size portions of Jedi whoop-ass.

The adrenalin rush of seeing such cinematic luminaries as Samuel L

Jackson and Christopher Lee throwing themselves into gravity defying battles

that make The Matrix look like it had crashed are complemented by the

almost balletic choreography and beautifully abstract visuals. Even the addition of

hundreds of Jedi fighting doesn't saturate the senses, with each duel more

exciting than anything in the series to date.

When it is at it's best Attack Of The Clones not only looks truly

amazing, it feels truly amazing too. It has moments where it totally immerses

you in another world. However these successes are punctuated by a

mundane teenage love story that makes Dawson's Creek seem racy and an unsatisfying ending designed to lead into the sequel. The rabble-rousing action-scenes will satisfy viewers who came for the thrill-ride experience and as part

of the series Attack Of The Clones is an excellent linking episode, but

viewed in isolation this is merely a slightly superior blockbuster.

title: Has Lucas Turned to the dark side?
review:
There are two ways of looking at `Attack of the Clones'. In correlation with the Star Wars saga then it is just about passable as a film that keeps the momentum of the precedent films going. However, as a film in itself it is a lame, laughable attempt at a summer blockbuster. It fits the codes and conventions of all big-budget Hollywood movies(this is not a compliment), the majority of the budget was clearly spent on the action sequences, which to be fair, are the best in any of the Star Wars films. However, the screenplay was so terrible that it would look out of place in an American daytime soap opera. There is one crucial thing that George Lucas must realise; George,YOU CANT WRITE SCRIPTS AND YOUR EAR FOR DIALOGUE IS NON-EXISTENT!!!(There, now I'm vented). Also I have to know what Lucas was smoking when he cast Hayden Christensen as Anakin Skywalker.I thought Jar-Jar Binks was as bad as it got in Star Wars, I was tragically wrong. In another review of this film, it said that Christensen acted as if he had just come out of Dawson's Creek. I find that statement far too complimentary (and anyway, I like Dawson's Creek!).I found his performance more immature and childish than Jake Lloyd's in The Phantom Menace, he behaved like a spoilt kid who didn't get a Playstation 2 for Christmas. It fills me with trepidation that Christensen will be reprising the role in Episode III, I don't see how he can convince when he makes the transformation from Anakin to Darth Vader.

While the storyline itself moved along fairly well, there were solid performances from Ewan McGregor, Samuel.L.Jackson and even Natalie Portman, who had a thankless task in the romance sequence with Anakin. Lucas has never handled romance in his films before. On this evidence, I can see why:he obviously doesn't know how!

The main strength of this movie is the action. The light sabre battle between Yoda and Count Dooku must surely rank as one of the greatest fights in cinematic history. However, this doesn't hide that `Attack of the Clones' is nothing better than average.

On a broader scale, what is most worrying is that Lucas clearly sacrificed art for spectacle. His only focus seemed to be the action scenes, while plot development took a back seat. He has pandered to the demands of Hollywood while leaving movie fans hungry for him to reproduce his best work. For Lucas to end the Star Wars saga in the manner in which he started it, he must go back and look at the initial Star Wars films to remind him how it should be done, or better yet, Lord of the Rings.

Myself, as a fan, got chuckles and warm feelings inside at the re-uttering of classic lines, musical cues, and of course character cameos.  Sometimes Lucas intently or not steps over the line and movie becomes more about giving props and filling the notions of what if and wouldnt it be cool if instead of creating a good story.  But this can be easily forgiven because it is fun to watch these flies of fancy. title: (Almost) no Jar-Jar to blame this time.
review:
I have two main problems with Episode II: the dialogue and the plot.

The dialogue never had to be stellar - people don't go to Lucas films for Shakespeare - but somewhere along the line it became really really awful. Stupid puns everywhere you go, and verbal references to lines popular with the older crowd ("I've got a bad feeling about this", "you're going to be the death of me"). The plot annoyed me not because of the broad sweep of things (we all know what has to happen before the end of Episode III, and Lucas has to get that going), but because of Lucas's need to explain *every little thing*. Why bring in Jango Fett? Why keep introducing C3PO and R2-D2? Is it so incredible that in a galaxy of (presumably) hundreds of billions of sentient (and suspiciously humanoid) beings, a few of them might just slip through the cracks, and not be seen again? It seems pointless to me, and complicates the overall story too much.

I didn't actually think the underlying acting was too bad. Christensen wasn't that bad, and Portman was OK, too. Though apart from youth and proximity, I'm not sure where the chemistry between them was supposed to come from. The real irritant for me was McGregor. He certainly *can* act, and he was one of the bright points of Episode I. His character is supposed to mature from a callow youth to wise old Alec-Guinness Obi-Wan. And yet all he seems to have done by now is grow a beard and become heavier-set. He seems unnecessarily stupid (as others have pointed out) and pompous. Perhaps this is a plot necessity, but it's irritating as hell, and I don't know where it's coming from. Now I know that Star Wars should have ended with Return of the Jedi. It's funny how pretty bad stuff can give you the warm fuzzies of nostalgia after enough time had passed. I recall thinking that Ewoks were a bad move in the (retitled) Episode VI, but really that was just a warmer up. Lucas is just making kiddie films with lots of violence and incredible CGI.

Oh, and on a more childish note, there's lots of lightsaber fighting, but none of it seems as good as the two extended scenes in Phantom Menace.

title: Lucas regains his stride
review:
Forget about the mediocre acting, forget about the occasionally clunky dialouge. This is Star Wars and it's judged on different merits than other movies. It's a part of a sweeping epic. It's to be judged in large part for it's contribution to the mythology. And besides the franchise owes so much to cheesy Saturday matinees of long ago that your really missing the point if your looking for high caliber performances.

This movie draws you in to its stunning visuals and epic story. The ever present CGI is supposed to turn you off if you're a serious person who truly appreciates film. In reality it's an amazing tool. Lucas has created worlds out of thin air, worlds that make you want to hop the next ship to Coursicant. Every last action scene is first rate. You know your watching something better than the Phantom Menace once the chase through the skies of Coursicant is underway. If this had happened in the Phantom Menace we'd have had some tow headed scamp shout "Wa-Hoo" 30 seconds into it. And Yoda gives us the best and most creatively depicted Light Saber fight yet.

It's not lacking for story either. The Phantom Menace attempted to draw dramatic weight from political intriuge and failed. The tactic works here, in large part because the entire film more mature. The love story is sub-Pearl-Harbour material. But it makes more sense as the film ends. And it gets us where we're going, so why complain? Anakin here is portrayed as having gone over to the Whiney Side, but there quite a few good scenes that make his eventual fall to evil believable. And Palpatine oozes menace, but not so much that you wonder how Amadala could trust him.

This movie may be the second best of the five. Lucas either always had it in him and simply mis-stepped with the Phantom Menace, or he understood the critisism of it and took it seriously. Or it could be both. The Phantom Menace made me angry, The Attack of the Clones makes me want to go back and watch the originals.

title: Better than Episode 1, but.....
review:
Well, I saw the film a few days after it came out, and, like many of my fellow fans, I was eagerly awaiting it. After Episode 1 I was hoping the this film would be heads above. Then I saw the film.

Some of the things I liked about this film are the same ones that everyone has mentioned, namely the Yoda battle scene. However, this one scene cannot make up for the rest of the film. Really, the rest of the film let me down.

The acting was stiff and the lines were poorly written, which, combined, means the the delivery of many lines bordered on horrible. The language used when writing the film has become more and more casual. Common everyday expressions are peppered within the script and slapstick comedy are all too common.

Even though I am a fan, there were way too many winks-to-the-fans within this film. While I enjoyed the first couple of jokes they become too much by the end. Especially with such a convoluted plot. At the end of Empire there were lots of loose ends, but not plain confusion like the end of this film.

I guess the main thing I disliked about this film was the 50's diner scene. My respect for the Star Wars universe had never been so shaken nor reduced until I saw this scene. There is just no need for the scene and it reduces the calibur of the film.

While this film was a major step in the right direction, it is still not quite right. Beautiful graphics, CG, and scenery will never make up for an excellent script or good acting, a lesson that seems to have been forgotten at times over at the Skywalker ranch. Hopefully if the second episode can be so much better then the first then the third may finally be up to expected par.

-Christopher

title: An Uninspired Attack on Fan Loyalty!
review:
I am a die hard fan; have been since I was eight. Speaking as such, it's my opinion that the truth about Lucas having three completed trilogies and only showing us the middle one is nothing more than a line he used in film school to pick up chics.

When Episode I debuted I was filled with a sense of awe, which quickly turned to "ahh crap". I realized Episode I was, for the most part, like its predecessor Return of the Jedi; a two hour toy commercial with a video game pitch. Only this time, instead of Ewoks George pushed child actors and toddler aliens on us.

I can almost forgive the poorly acted, uninspired dialogue. If it weren't for the glarring potholes in the plot. For example; Jenja Fett is hired to assasinate Amidala, which he subcontracts out to a female, assian shape shifter...who then deploys a droid?! Oh, and the MOST POWERFUL JEDI to ever live doesn't sense a disturbance until the WORMS are hanging over her?! When his first attempt fails, Jenja simply gives up and goes home. Poof, no more attempts on Amadaila's life. Oh, since when can R2D2 fly?! That would have come in handy on Tantooine...guess he just likes doing things the hard way. I won't espouse my distates for the poorly execuited, hackneyed attempt at a romance between Anakin and Amadala. Obi-wan Kenobi entrusts the life of a high-ranking politcal figure to his inexperienced, hot-headed student so he can hop around the galaxy playing detective?

I've heard alot of fans going on and on about the special effects. Big deal! Special effects in a Star Wars movie are as common place as popcorn in a movie theatre. Why should anyone be awed. It's a given! Even Lucas has fallen into the trap. He's like a kid in a candy store. It seems to me that he spent more time digitally animating Yoda than he did writing his dialogue. It's supposed to be about the story!!!

I was under the impression that the Prequel Trilogies of Star Wars would explore the motivations and path leading to the creation of the Sinister Darth Vader. So far, George Lucas is 2 for 0. What a galactic disapointment. The Anakin Skywalker I'm seeing on the silver screen could never grow up to become the meanace of the galaxy we all feared and admired, the Man who cuts off his own son's hand to win a lightsaber duel and bring him into the evil fold.

title: Cinematic Grand Opera
review:
Attack of the Clones is an impressive experience as we have all come to expect from each new film in the Star Wars saga. Visual effects, sound, and music all combine to deliver a glorious spectacle. Even though I knew ahead of time that all these elements would be spectacular, nothing that came before really prepared me for this when I sat down to actually see the film. As pure magic show, the Star Wars films have time and again proven their worth. It should be noted that the film is only truly appeciated in a large theater properly equipped with digital projection and well balanced digital sound systems.

But, as with the last two Star Wars films that have been made, Return of the Jedi and The Phantom Menace, I came away feeling that George should have hired me to polish the screenplay. In as much as this can be taken for criticism (and of an arrogant kind), it is really a tribute, for Lucas has created something so remarkable that most movie goers, from the casual observer to the rabid fan alike, can hardly resist the desire to invest something of themselves in it.

As is the case in general with the Star Wars phenomenon, it should be noted that yes, these are just movies, and everyone seems rather inclined to make too much of them. But, because it is such an undeniable phenomenon, perhaps no script, no matter how brilliant, could hope to live up to everyone's expectations.

Be that as it may, I would say that since A New Hope and The Empire Strikes Back, Lucas has failed to get the most out of his material and his story telling opportunity. The bottom line is that while his instincts for character and story are sound, he simply lets too many elements crowd his vision. His fascination with technology and cinematic canvassing has more often than not overwhelmed his characters and their story.

This film is very exciting and thrilling stuff, make no mistake. It is as entertaining as one might hope for, albeit maybe a bit relentless. I would have preferred it if some of the protracted action scenes earlier in the film had been curtailed a few minutes here and there to give the characters and themes some more breathing room. This might also have served to give the stunning, climactic battle scenes an even greater impact.

I would disagree straight away with those who dismiss the Star Wars saga as plot-less. Lucas really has created a very imaginative and engrossing space opera with splendid archetypal characters, mythological undercurrents, and universal themes. As in all good re-tellings of the same basic human stories, these themes are played out with important and timely relevancies.

The Star Wars saga is routinely criticized for its portentous dispensation of philosophy, religion, politics, and science. But if anything, I think Lucas might be criticized for being too reticent to give these elements fuller play. No doubt, the greatest difficulty for him as he has unfolded his saga has been to somehow meld these engrossing operatic elements in a way that does not diminish the work as it was also meant to be - a fun Saturday afternoon serial adventure story. This difficulty is something that few of his harsher critics fully appreciate. Maybe it's just me, but I think the philosophies and politics of the Star Wars galaxy lends as much to its fascination as does its spectacular settings, vehicles, weapons, and life forms. This remains true as much for me when I saw A New Hope at the age of 12 as does Attack of the Clones at 37.

The old Flash Gordon serials were clear inspiration for the young George Lucas, but he has created something far larger than anything the old B-movie moguls could have dreamed of. And I am not speaking of just production values here. By injecting more than imagination and excitement into these films, Lucas elevated the material onto a more seriously engaging stage.

Thus, I must say that where Attack of the Clones has come up short, like the two proceeding films, has been in the near impossibility of trying to combine, if you will, elements of grand opera with light musical comedy in the same dramatic context. While this strange and intoxicating blend worked so well in Episodes IV and V, it has been a much more difficult thing to achieve in the later installments, primarily because so much more emphasis has been placed on ratcheting up the GRAND factor.

It is worth noting that the definition of `grand' opera, as opposed to opera of the ordinary sort, is not so much in the depth and seriousness of the material, but more with the opulence of its presentation. Grand Opera as a style was popular within the decadent French culture of the 18th and 19th centuries. These grandiose musical plays provided heaps of evening entertainment for the theatre going public of their day, but they were little performed afterwards and not just because of the production expense. Sparing no expense has rarely ever turned away theater goers. The real reason that these works lost their audience was that once the novelty of the presentation wore off, or they were surpassed by something grander still, they were found in time to be.too boring.

It was Richard Wagner alone among opera composers who achieved a workable balance of grand opera and engaging drama. His theatrical epics are portentous, no question, but compellingly so. And it was no accident that Wagner found his inspiration within the great treasure of medieval mythology. It is probably safe to say that without the example of Tristan and Isolde, Parsifal, and The Ring of the Nibelung, there would be no Star Wars, or Lord of the Rings either for that matter.

What is also interesting is that like Lucas, Wagner found the technical means at his disposal entirely inadequate to his purposes. Wagner's specially constructed Bayreuth Festival Theatre was the THX cinema of its time, the only way that The Ring in particular could be presented in any kind of convincing fashion.

Gratefully, Lucas does not appear to be nearly so full of himself as Wagner and while Star Wars may not be in the same league with the greatest of grand operas in terms of its richness as art and drama, it similarly commands the fascination and excitement of the public. Just as Wagner's operas were a popular phenomenon of their time, they also advanced the technique and power of the dramatic experience.

Star Wars is very much regarded as a pure form of contemporary `pop culture'. Wagner's music dramas were blockbusters too, but today, they can no longer be considered popular. The number of people who have seen a Wagner opera are infinitesimal compared to the number who have seen major films and Broadway stage shows. Yet, Wagner's best grand operas continue to hold their own for those that know them, just as the best Star Wars films do, by the measure with which their stories are developed and the sophistication of the technique by which they are presented.

As so many film critics are at pains to point out, the B-movie formula of old is now the industrial mainstay of the modern film business to the complete degeneration of the medium as a serious vehicle for drama and art. George Lucas is widely regarded as the person most responsible for this state of affairs. In the first place, this whole argument is without perspective. Hollywood has always churned out a steady stream of pulp material and always will. It is a business after all.

If there is any reason why we as movie lovers might expect Lucas to somehow deliver something greater and more memorable than the usual popcorn fodder, it is simply because he has done it before. In the first two Star Wars films Lucas achieved something more remarkable than spectacle - he transcended formula with a powerful Wagnerian combination of mythos and rich audio-visual palette. Lucas brought a different set of instincts to the screen with Star Wars. I think the real intent was not so much to conjure up such elements that would sell more movie tickets, but how to re-tell the tales of old in a new and compelling way. These creative instincts are what made Star Wars something special and what I think really accounts for its huge success.

Without question, the enormity of its success has profoundly changed the ways of the movie business, but it has also had its impact on Lucas himself, as it would certainly be expected to.

With all the means and, more importantly, freedoms at his disposal, we might not be too guilty if we should come to expect him to fulfill the greater promise of this saga.

As with Return of the Jedi and The Phantom Menace there is again in Attack of the Clones a small sense of nagging disappointment. It is a pity that the same incredible exertion of talent and energy that has gone into making each new episode in the Star Wars saga such a spectacular and detailed audio-visual feast could not also have been brought to bear on enriching the finer details of the screenplay.

On some level it must be conceded that the Star Wars saga has a life of its own, and in this sense really is more than just a series of entertaining movies. It has all the elements of grand opera at its best and I think Lucas might have made the mistake along the way of thinking that his audience wants only to be entertained.

The only other criticism I would level at Lucas is that while his casting has been by and large quite fine, he has not come to fully realize that his actors, no matter how good, need greater attention when they are being asked to play characters within the context of such an epic story and within such a fantastic environment. The environment for them in particular is a great challenge and not just because it is invisible to them when they are performing. It rests on their shoulders to convey and maintain the human dimension amidst such glorious spectacle.

On this point, I think Lucas owes a significant debt to his composer John Williams. The exciting and brilliant underscore he provides for all the many action sequences is often lost in the exotic and dense mixture of great sound effects, but in those brief moments when the characters are in close up, he greatly helps bolster the overshadowed human element.

Lucas's saga is very character driven, but in his approach to getting this on film, I would say a fair measure of it is being lost in translation.

He has for all intents and purposes turned the whole process of film production on its head. With most films the largest phase of their making is labelled `production', or what is essentially principal photography. `Post-Production' typically refers to the process of stitching all the assembled pieces together. In the case of Star Wars, and especially so in this new era of computer generated visualization, principal photography is now the smallest phase. Far more time, energy, and money is poured into Post-Production - so much so that it is a complete misnomer to refer to it as such. What this has meant for the actors and their characters is that they have taken on that rather sketchy quality of `Pre-Production' elements.

Film critics complain, and not entirely without merit, that technology is rendering the role of actors and their characters less important. Yet, in another sense, this wrongly suggests that they should necessarily be more important. No medium lends itself so well to make-believe as film. One should not find fault in the simple fact that the technical means of the medium are at this time reaching a real maturity.

Maybe the issue is that technology has not advanced nearly far enough. Would it not be a great thing for human actors to able to interface more directly with the splendid verisimilitude modern cinematic techniques provide? For gifted actors, I think this would a great boon. Maybe someday, and maybe not too far away if Lucasfilm continues to progress things as they do, the actors will come in for what is now the real `Production' phase and enter the `set' through some means of virtual reality.

As Anakin Skywalker represents the failed hope of his world to bring it the balance it so needs, he nonetheless through his striving lays the groundwork for a future generation to realize it, so George Lucas is giving filmmakers the means to do things never before possible, and if Lucas himself is not entirely able to bring fullest balance to these powerful new cinematic methods, it will be the essential challenge of present and future filmmakers to do so.

In spite of its narrative short comings, the Star Wars saga remains the measure by which all fantasy adventure films must be judged. Attack of the Clones is no exception and without a doubt Lucas has progressed, and continues to progress, the capabilities of the medium of film to ever new dizzying heights. Many will argue critically - to what real or greater purpose? The proof is in the pudding. Star Wars is delightful and delicious stuff. And as far as many of its essential production elements are concerned, particularly in the case its production design, costume design, visual effects, music, and editing, it gives as much credence to cinema as an art form as does anything else.

What is perhaps most strange of all is the incongruity that now exists within the saga itself. The chronologically earlier episodes have a technical polish and sophistication that all but dwarfs the experience one has watching the later episodes, made as they were with such comparatively antiquated techniques. In the best of all possible cinematic universes, we might have the glorious technical spectacle of Phantom Menace and Attack of the Clones with the tighter narrative and fuller character development found in A New Hope and Empire Strikes Back. Here's hoping that Lucas himself can bring that balance back to the Force in Episode III - for which we must now patiently wait three long years.

title: Uh... craaap!
review: Aside from the special effects and the intriguing origins of the great Boba Fett, this movie stinks to high heavens (yes, even those in a galaxy far, far away). Jar Jar Binks is given mercifully little screen time, but any screen time for that abomination is a crime against humanity. George Lucas should think about making some other films every now and then. He has seriously lost his way with this landmark franchise, and seems hellbent on completely obliterating his own legacy.

title: Up There
review: If you liked Empire Strikes Back, then you can think of EII as a better version (but for the first trilogy). I won't give major plot elements but I can tell you everyone plays thier role well. I will tell you that Jango Fett has a very important role in the movie. You will enjoy this movie, defentitly if you are in any way a Star Wars fan. Probably a B+ to a A for a non-Star Wars fan, a A+ for a Star Wars fan. Go see it, you will love it.

title: The Force is back!
review: Since i can remember my self,i've been a great Star Wars fan!I can watch all the movies (yes,EVEN Episode I!) without get bored and every time i like them more and more.I'm not the kind of fun that collects every toy that comes out or stuff like that.I like the movies and their plot,the way that they are made,the feeling that every movie provides... I belong to the fans that were a bit dissapointed by Episode I but i knew that this was only the beginning and that in some years i was going to see one of the best Star Wars movies! I went to the theater to watch a Star Wars movie,to be taken in this familiar universe and have some wonderfull moments.And i was not dissapointed this time...Attack of the Clones is wonderfull made,from the beginning till the end!The story is better than Episode I and the characters have more depth.Ewan McGregor and Hayden Christensen are making an incredible duo,the way they speak and act is very enjoyable! I've read some bad reviews about the chemistry between Christensen and Natalie Portman,but i think that it is set up vey good.It is not Shakespeare,it is not even Titanic but it's ok,just ok,a very good love story in the Star Wars universe.And i don't want to hear anything about comparissons with the classic trilogy!It is the new trilogy and it has a totally new feeling,that is to be expected! My only instance about the movie has to do something with the greatest actor that AOTC has:Christofer Lee.In this final scene,where he challenges Yoda into a lightsaber duel it seems like Lucas wrote it just to please the fans.I mean,what do the fans awaited all the years?To see once Yoda fighting!And Lucas writes a very cheesy dialogue for Christofer Lee's role and it seems like Count Dooku is only there to announce something like "Hey,fans,this is what you have waiting for!See Yoda fighting!".This is my only instance,because when the fight begins,WOW,it was really something never seen before!Good job! I don't know,i would like to tell more but without give any more spoiklers,it's a bit difficult.The movie rocks,it is the movie every Star Wars fan,hardcore or not,wanted to see.It has fun,it has emotion, it has darkness and,yes,it has mistakes but,hell,it is Star Wars that you are watching to!A must for the fans.Well,other people can se it too but only after watching at least Episode I.I rated this movie 10/10 and i can't wait till 2005 for Episode III!

title: Mediocre
review:
Great special effects and dazzling monsters can't make me like the latest piece of the Star Wars epic, but they certainly tried. Of course, some people enjoy Star Wars films precisely for this reason and I can't argue with that. However, if you like your films to contain a well-written script, believable characters, good acting, and chemistry then look elsewhere as this movie fails miserably.

The original trilogy contained all of these things and were a joy to behold. Somehow, George Lucas has lost the ability to develop characters that resonate with me. I can't speak for others but I suspect that many people feel the same way. My wife was quick to point out the non-existent chemistry between Anakin and Padme and I noticed other failed connections between the characters. Including Samuel L. Jackson and Jimmy Smits into the cast was distracting as I kept thinking about 'pulp fiction' and 'NYPD Blue' every time they appeared. Oh well, at least there *were* cool looking monsters and creatures to look at and the "5th Element" looking cities with air traffic weren't bad. This film should have been so much more...5 out of 10.

title: Attack of the Groans.......
review:
Let's be honest about things for a second...

Every one of the original trilogy was slated at some point by a large amount of people - these days, 20 years later, there are just more means to do it and therefore everyone has to voice an opinion somewhere...and to the people who sit in front of the PC slagging off the movie and pointing out the bad bits I say these 8 words...

IT'S ONLY A MOVIE FOR CRYING OUT LOUD!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!

To those of us who enjoy Star Wars for what it is i.e. ENTERTAINMENT, Episode II is a delicious slice of escapist wonder, exactly the same as the previous 4 episodes (Yes - I most certainly include Episode I in that statement!). It is never going to be perfect - show me a film that is? for those people who don't like it - FINE! GO AND MAKE A BETTER MOVIE!!!!! (Oops, sorry Mr Spielberg!)

It is a movie that encompasses, and enhances, elements of all 4 previous outings, and takes them to the next step...OK, so people think the script ain't up to much - and to those people I say look at the original Star Wars (Or A New Hope for the purists, if you insist) - the script was far worse then!! Characters? Everyone laughed out loud at the droids in that movie - in fact fans have had something to moan about in each of the movies (Jedi Master is a MUPPET!!!! Galaxy saved by TEDDY BEARS!!!!!). In fact that brings me to the one PERSONAL dislike of Ep II - the somewhat IN MY OPINION misplaced humour, hence the title of my post...please notice that I emphasise IN MY OPINION - I am not trying, like many people on here, to ram my opinion down your throat.

To the people who don't like it I say FINE!!! Go and watch something else you DO enjoy! But if you have nothing better to do than go on about how bad YOU think it is, you desperately need help my friends...

To the vast, vast majority of people out there who DO like Ep II, join me in shouting one big MR LUCAS, EPISODE III CAN NOT COME SOON ENOUGH!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!

title: A formula movie, but it is a billion dollar formula.
review: George Lucas has used the last quarter century to perfect the formula for the most successful franchise in film history. All the elements are present in just the right amounts to give a good two and a half hour diversion that lives up to past "Star Wars" installments. The performances are competent and adequate for the genre, but the villain turn delivered by eighty year old Christopher Lee was showy and over the top and very fun to watch. The music by old pro John Williams was familiar and contributed to the sense of sitting down with an old friend and covering familiar territory. In total a good movie, not a great movie; but one that delivers everything promised.

Anakin however does look upon Obewan Kenobi as his father he is also a rebelious teenager which has been shown to be a bad trait in a Jedi Knight and a additude that is not at all aloud.

title: Franchise's Fifth Finds Form
review:
There's nothing quite like a new "Star Wars" film to excite movie fans and, on the opening weekend at the première cinema in London, the sell-out audience was buzzing with expectation as we awaited the familiar theme tune and introductory sloping text. When it came, the folk applauded and hooted with pleasure. There is a family tradition of two decades whereby I take my son Rich to the new "Star Wars" movie and, although he is now in his mid-twenties and a fully fledged Jedi knight, we still honour that tradition - and it was just as well because, on occasions, this 50-something fan needed a bit of explanation of a convoluted plot.

I liked "The Phantom Menace", but "AOTC" will appeal more to aficionados, not least because - like the middle film in the second trio, "The Empire Strikes Back" - it is altogether darker, both metaphorically and visually. I'm becoming used to Ewan McGregor's weird accent as Obi-Wan Kenobi and lobeless but lovely Natalie Portman is a delight as Padmé Amidila. However, it is Canadian newcomer Hayden Christensen who has the most challenging role as 19 year old Anakin Skywalker, a personality in transition, constantly torn between the light and dark side of The Force. When he describes the savaging of the Tusken Raiders who killed his mother, one is reminded of the massacre scene towards the end of "Lawrence Of Arabia".

As always, George Lucas' fifth in the franchise is a technical tour de force. In the course of some 2,200 effects shots, we encounter wonderfully inventive worlds and weapons and a marvellous array of characters and creatures, all enhanced with stunning visuals and superb sound. Again as always, the weakest part of the production is the dialogue which reduced the audience to unintended laughter at several points. As Harrison Ford allegedly told Lucas on one of the earlier films: "George, you can type this s***, but you sure can't say it". On the other hand, Lucas was inspired to create the "Star Wars" saga by the Saturday matinee serials like "Flash Gordon" and their scripts were even worse.

At the end of the day, "AOTC" is not fine art but simple entertainment and, on that level, it certainly delivers with a roller-coaster ride and a thrilling finale that features - the best bit of the movie - Yoda kicking ass with Count Dooku. Personally I can't wait for 2005 and Episode III.

title: What happens when you market a film for all audiences.
review: Well this is an excellent study in what happens when a director tries to make a film that offers something for everyone, basically catering to all demographics. The result is at times inevitably mixed. Episode 2 remains true to the franchise but at the same time has perhaps what true purists might consider a bit too much of a romantic subplot. This in and of itself is not truly a bad thing but the script and lines could certainly have used some work in this department as most of the lines come off as corny or sappy. This is frustrating as you'll frequently find yourself laughing when one probably shouldn't be. Lucas does make up for this however with more than adequate doses of action and a genuinely intriguing storyline as one would expect. Don't expect to be swept off your feet when you walk into the theater as you might with the common whiz bang explosion openings most common in action films today but rather give the film time to mature and you should leave the theater thoroughly satisfied. When Clones is good it's GREAT, but when it's bad it's horrendous. However, from the looks of things Lucas is back on track with this overall greatly appreciated addition to the series.

title: Enjoyed it; purists wouldn't
review: First, I thoroughly enjoyed watching Star Wars, Episode II - the visual effects were spectacular, and though I had seen the first installment, I would have appreciated it just as much with no prior Star Wars knowledge. It says something about George Lucas that he can make it supply the vital links between parts past and future, as well as making the film a decent stand-alone piece. The film also made me laugh. Star Wars purists would be appalled by this - surely the genre is meant to be full of meaning, metaphor and sincerity. I'm more flexible myself, however there are only so many times that yet another character or force joins a single battle (which we had been led to believe was won, yet again) before it descends into something slightly ridiculous. The cinema erupted in hysterics in master yoda's fight scene - surely not the intention of the director? I think maybe Lucas was trying too hard to 'fill in the gaps' and provide viewers with an easy guide to who's going to be who in future - Obi Wan's comment to his troublesome pupil 'you're going to be the death of me' after a high-octane chase scene bordered on the poststructuralist surreal.  Having said that, though, I appreciate Lucas had a difficult job to do, which he performed to aplomb - making the movie exciting when anyone who has seen 'Star Wars' (don't read on if you haven't) knows damn well that Obi Wan, Yoda and Anakin will survive in order to feature in the original films. Despite knowing that she must survive in order to conceive Luke, I was still enthralled watching Senator Amidala's struggle to survive. In all, then, a film definitely worth watching - just suspend your sense of disbelief, and avoid being pedantic, and Star Wars II: Attack of the Clones is one of those films you can just sit back and enjoy, regardless of the occasional ludicrousies. Mind you, it would have been far better with some good acting - I am an actor and director myself and can imagine how hard it is to act against a character whose presence is only digitally added later, but even taking that into account, the standard of acting was, on the whole, sub-soap opera level, which even the cinema audience picked up on (more hysterical laughter) when Amidala suddenly and unconvincingly declared 'aaah...ahhh, er, I'm fine' on the desert sands towards the end. Nevertheless, a forcefully fun film to watch.

title: Are you people crazy?
review:
At the time of writing this, my first ever IMDB review, 'E2: Attack of the Clones' has a rating of 8.1. This is just plain nuts, and can not stand. One of the best things about IMDB is the rating system. It allows us, the users to get a good idea of what sort of experience we are in for. I fear the ratings are becoming worthless when this film has an 8.1.

This film has no plot, no protagonist, a barely there antagonist, sluggish editing, wooden acting, horrible dialogue, bad characterization, and unfulfilling action sequences. Other then that I guess it's OK.

To call this film a dog is an insult to all canine. It's more aptly described as Herpes. Ugly, no fun, and keeps coming back. Also, dumb people keep exposing themselves to it.

The best part of this film was the trailer for the Matrix: Reloaded that preceded it. Speaking of the Matrix, Hayden Christensen (Anakin Skywalker) makes Keanu Reeves look like the second coming of Robert De Niro. Everything about this kid is bad. There is nothing subtle or complex about his performance. He comes off as nothing more than a whiney, spoiled teenager. He's just a little less irritating then Jar Jar Binks, who's every word makes me long for a Monty Python like Light saber accident that results in the lopping off of Binks' head.

This film seems to have been created for children. Everything is so overt. Remember the mystique of the exotic characters of the first three movies? Where are the exotic languages? Where are the subtitles? No instead we get big fat alien fry cooks with Brooklyn accents, and little hairy ones with buzzing flies and Italian accented English. What a joke.

The special effects were stunning, but that does not make a movie. In fact it seems apparent in this case it may actually kill it. Give me the early '80s technology of the first three movies with a decent plot and good acting any day.

Please understand. I was a big fan. I stood in line for hours with my dad when I was 10 years old to see the first one. I stood in line for hours to see the re-release of the first three with my wife in '96-'97. I had the action figures. I had the plastic Light saber. I even put up with my little brother's watching those damn Ewok shows. But the line is drawn here!

title: **1/2 (out of ****)
review:
I tried George. I tried to like. I wanted to like it, really I did. I grew up with the original "Star Wars" trilogy, and wanted so desperately to like "Attack of the Clones", especially after I desperately tried to like "The Phantom Menace". But alas, I just could not. There simply was not enough there for me to like.

I recently watched "The Phantom Menace" again, to bring myself up to speed again (I guess) for Episode II. The problem with that film was Jar Jar Binks' ability to irritate the most die-hard and optimistic of Star Wars fans, and an unconvincing little Anakin (played by Jake Lloyd). Episode II is an improvement then, simply because there is no little kid, and Jar Jar's role is minimal.

The film opens ten years after the events in Episode I; Anakin Skywalker (now played by Hayden Christiansen) is no longer a tyke, but in his late teens, filled with almost as much teen angst as he had in "Life as a House". Padme Amidala (Natalie Portman) is no longer Queen, but a senator and Obi-Wan (Ewan McGregor) has grown a beard and needs a hair cut. Much of the first act of the film is comprised of `what have you been up to?' dialogue.

Anyway, there is an assassination attempt of Senator Amidala, and Obi-Wan and Anakin are dispatched by the Jedi Council to protect her and investigate. We learn that Anakin has dreamed of Padme every day since he last saw her ten years ago, and is hopelessly in love with her. Padme, though, hides her feelings.

The plot thickens when Obi-Wan stumbles on a planet that is producing millions of Clone Troopers (which look suspiciously like Storm Troopers). At the same time, plagued by nightmares, Anakin returns to Tatooine in search of his mother.

Now there is nothing really wrong with the story, just the execution of said story is extremely poor. What Lucas really needed was to hire someone to touch up the screenplay (perhaps Lawrence Kasdan again? He did co-write "Empire" and "Jedi"). Some of the dialogue, especially between Christiansen and Portman is downright atrocious. It has none of the wit or verve of anything in the original trilogy, and at times sounds remarkably like a bad high school play. Their relationship feels awkward and decidedly forced (pun intended suckers!). The romance is even more disappointing in comparison to the romance between Han Solo and Princess Leia, and how it developed with ease and effortless charm.

Portman does her best with the material, but it is Christiansen who is the dead weight. He plays Anakin like a grumpy 12 year-old in many scenes. In one scene particularly, feelings of remorse and fear would have been suitable and moving, instead he throws a temper tantrum. Christiansen delivers his lines with such banality, there is little interest for, and not much to like about his character. Perhaps though, he is not meant to be liked, after all he does become Darth Vader, the most notorious screen villain in history. But at the same time how could he not be interesting? I mean he is Darth Vader! Well, Christiansen and Lucas found a way.

Most of the elements we've come to expect from the Star Wars franchise are here: gorgeous special effects, light saber duels, grand battles, and John Williams' score. What's missing, though, is a sense of fun; a sense of awe and wonder. Perhaps it's because the story is mundane and sophomoric. It feels tired, like everyone involved just wanted to get it done and over with; even Williams' score is sub par.

To me it seems Lucas is more concerned with getting the story told, rather than relishing in telling the story of the rise and fall of Anakin Skywalker. Much of the film, despite its running time of 142 minutes, feels rushed, especially the final 15 minutes or so.

The film does have some high points, though not enough. There's a fun speeder chase (of sorts) through the towering city of Coruscant, there are some amusing moments with R2-D2 and C-3PO, and the final battle of clones, Jedi and droids is pure eye candy. With the exception of the speeder chase (which occurs early), we have to sit through 80 minutes of clumsy exposition and set up, much of which for the next film. Hopefully the third and final prequel will finally pay off, and reach the heights of the original trilogy.

title: Finally! A 12 on a scale of 10.
review: Attack of the Clones has an excellent balance not often seen in action/adventure/fantasy movies, which is a balanced approach to character development. Mixing action with plenty of intimate portrayls, panoramic vistas and less dialog have made this movie a masterpiece of artistic expression. More that just entertaining; the mythology, such as it is, has reached an inspired peak that over time will make its own mark in the American personality. The visionary aspect of the movie is breathtaking. Compared to the typical, shallow, self serving Hollywood junk (that is often a weak attempt at political self-gratification) this movie is on a completely superior scale in every way.

title: Quit your whining...
review:
Yea, Ep. II has some bad dialogue and a contrived love story, but IT'S STAR WARS for crying out loud! If you're like me, you've been waiting since 1983 for another Star Wars movie, and you've got 2 so far. Sadly, all those "hardcore" Star Wars fans think that they're better than George Lucas, when most of them don't know what the outside of their parent's basement looks like.

Anyway, onto the film.

Dialogue - Like all movies, it comes off a bit wooden every once and a while. Some of the humor falls flat, some works perfectly. I think when Anakin and Obi-Wan are chasing Zam through Coruscant has some nice wit that most would consider stupid. The dialogue between Anakin and Padme when the arrive at the lake is really bad. The best bit though is in the room on Tatooine when Anakin comes back from the Tusken camp w/ Padme. That's powerful.

SFX - Absolutely stuning. Coruscant's cityscape is amazing. The Asteroid Field is wonderful, specially w/ the seismic charges. Geonosis is a nice wasteland. And so on and so forth. The clonetroopers are quite cool looking CG.

Plot - Complaining about a lack of plot you say? Look, and you shall see. Yea, it's convoluted, but it's not nearly as bad as 95% of all summer movies Hollywood puts out. It's an engaging plot line, cept for the lackluster romance.

Overall - This movie is better than "The Phantom Menace" and is still very much Star Wars as TPM was. Can't wait for Episode III in 2005.

title: Finally! A 12 on a scale of 10.
review: Attack of the Clones has an excellent balance not often seen in action/adventure/fantasy movies, which is a balanced approach to character development. Mixing action with plenty of intimate portrayls, panoramic vistas and less dialog have made this movie a masterpiece of artistic expression. More that just entertaining; the mythology, such as it is, has reached an inspired peak that over time will make its own mark in the American personality. The visionary aspect of the movie is breathtaking. Compared to the typical, shallow, self serving Hollywood junk (that is often a weak attempt at political self-gratifcation) this movie is on a completely superiour scale in every way.

title: Laughably bad dialogue
review:
It's really, really sad when you're sitting in a theater with 1000 non-native English speakers and they're laughing at the amazingly cliched, poorly read English dialogue. The scene with Anakin moaning "mother" in bed elicited shrieks of laughter, and, upon reflection, is the only really memorable scene in the entire film.

As one Finnish girl remarked after the film was over, "the cheese is strong with this one."

title: Pretty pictures but dissapointing script & many plot holes
review:
I grew up on Star Wars and had all the original toys. Even though I am a fan of the old movies, these new ones deserve fair examination. Episode II : The CGI was beautiful, probably the most advanced to date. There was detail given to the environments. Some of the action scenes later in the movie were enthralling. However that did not save this movie. The most obvious problem is the dialogue which is pretty lame by any standard. Characters did not come across as real people, or at least anyone you cared about. Love scenes were amusing in the way of a cheap romance novel. People in the theater either laughed or groaned.

Ep. II plot holes : (Spoilers)

1. The only reason the Jedi found the million stormtroopers was because the planet was traced back from a dart left in a victim by Fett. Fett uses a blaster in every other scene, because it makes more sense. It's not like the dart was stealthier, he was still caught in the act.

2. It was ultimately convenient for the Jedi/Republic to find a million clones right when they needed them. An unknown Jedi ordered them 10 years ago and no one (including Jedi council) knew anything about it? I suppose he paid the $10000 trillion cost out of his own pocket. All the Jedi would have been killed by Dookuu's anrmy in the battle arena without this convenient plot developement, since the Senate never put together the army of the republic.

3. Annakin looks like he's 15 years older since the last movie but the princess looks right about the same age...

4. The aliens that made the clones had no problem talking to Obi-wan about the clone army (and later handing them over) despite Obi-wan being obviously ignorant about the whole deal. Fett knew that Obi-wan was ignorant after they talked in his room, why didn't Fett kill him then?

5. The battle driods. Do these useless things actually hit anybody in either episode I or II?! I mean if you are going to bother making driods that can walk and talk you figure they would throw in some targeting components, or maybe even a networking card so the little guys could work togther. If a 100 of them shot at one Jedi at a time they could have ended that area battle in short time.

6. Dookoo is not much of a master Jedi if he can't sense the the good guys coming.

7. Yoda limps throughout the whole movie and then goes hyper-ninja on Count Dookoo? It was fun to watch, but notice he goes right back to limping as soon as the action is over.

8. Why is this Princess so important? We havn't seen any important political action from her in either movie. What was so important about Naboo from the last movie? So the trade federation blocked her planet... What did they export that was so important to the whole galaxy?!

9. Because the Princess is such an important figure, they assign her to be guarded by a Jedi. Next thing, Obi-Wan takes off and leaves her with the padwan learner (Anakin) who is obviously terrible at following orders.

10. Why was Fett chosen to be the one that was cloned? We never see anything particularly special about him. The Jedi that made the order would choose such a shady character?

11. Instead of consulting experts, Obi-Wan asks the local chef who knew exactley where Fett's dart came from, and about the clone-making planet that no one else (including the Galactic Encylopedia and Jedi council) had ever heard of.

12. Yoda struggled to keep the giant piller from crushing Obi Wan and Anakin during the fight with Dookoo, but I remembered him saying that the size of the thing doesn't matter in Ep.5?

13. Anakin hasn't seen his mom in 10 years and races across the galaxy to find her. He finally rescues her from the Sandpeople but right then she dies. What was the point of that? ...I'm sure there are others but enough for now. Overall, the good parts were like watching the most advanced video game which is a cheap thrill in itself. The bad parts were those scenes where people were talking.

title: A masterpiece!
review: Before I went to see this movie two times, I was pretty certain that AOTC was destined to be the best in the Star Wars series, and I was right! I absolutely adore this movie. It has everything a Star Wars movie need: action, romance, suspense, a little humor, etc.. It was far superior than the TPM and it was well worth the wait, too. See it for yourself and I hope you'll enjoy this one as much as I did. Don't believe what all the critics are saying about AOTC, see it first, then decide for yourself if weather you liked it or not. Have fun! :)

title: The best
review:
As much as I defended Episode I, allot of elements of that film let me down. Episode II was fantastic. George Lucas realized with Episode I that he's no screenwriter, so he brought help and it worked out for the best. This film has some incredible action sequences, the FX are incredible. Each film makes me respect ILM a bit more. But what really made the film shine for me was the drama. I usually don't like love stories, especially ones involving teenagers (Titanic), but I have to say that I was impressed with this. Natalie Portman is certainly not an Oscar winner, but she has improved 10 fold since Phantom Menace. Hayden is amazing, he'll garner an Oscar in the next 5 years for sure. The jokes were mature and reminded me of Han Solo's brand of humor. ("Oh not good!"), even Jar Jar was great in this film. The film has that sense of adventure that I loved in Empire (Episode 5 in the series). The characters are rich and three-dimensional like the OT characters, well except for some of the politicians, but I believe that is by design. I've always loved the Jedi, they are my personal heroes in the SW Universe, and it was nice to really see them in action and in practice. We really got a glimpse of what life is like in the SW universe. None of the other films ever did that. Anakin's scene with his mother was an Oscar-calibre performance.

That said, EPisode II is not a film for Joe Sixpack. Most of the Star Wars films aren't for Joe Sixpack anymore. The action scenes, while incredible, are short and the film is mostly drama and love story, as are most of the SW films. Spider-Man is better suited to the action and comedy-centered needs of Joe Sixpack because the drama scenes are kept as short as possible.

Ever since we heard that Sam Jackson was gonna be in Star Wars we all wanted to see a bit of his Pulp Fictionesque hipper-than-thou attatitude, and we got to see that with lines like "This party's over," and his battle with Jango Fett.

The age-old question of why Yoda survives the Great Jedi Purge when all others die is answered. Anyone who doubts that Yoda could have survived wasn't paying attention. Anakin/Vader nor Palpatine could have challenged Yoda to a battle on any grounds and have expected to win.

But overall the only scene I really didn't like was Anakin's nightmare scene. I would have removed the dialogue and replaced it with some strangly familiar yet definately ambigious sounds, ending with a faint cry of help from his mother, Shmi Skywalker.

I'm someone who is throughoul familiar with Star Wars, I would qualify as one of the uber-geeks who knows every movie backwards and forwards, but I am also a filmmaker and I understand from that point of view as well. I really feel that Episode II is the best Star Wars film we have seen yet.

title: Finally.
review:
This review is littered with spoilers.

After how average the previous two movies were (The Phantom Menace and Return of the Jedi) Star Wars has made the return to the fun and greatness of the first two films (A New Hope and The Empire Strikes Back). THIS IS STAR WARS. Make no mistake about it. Everything just says Star Wars. Even the acting is more relaxed, and they're given more to do than just react to Liam Neeson. Lucas has been redeemed. He has made a great movie for the hardcore fans to love. I've heard at least a dozen fans say how much they love the movie and how it's better than TPM. However, the average movie goer might not be as happy as the fans, this film is more for the fans.

You can't deny that this film rules. A lot of the critics have forgotten how wooden the acting and bad the writing is in the first three movies. The action sequences are great, gone are primitive armies fighting advanced armies. We have battle droids from TPM vs. Clone Troopers (future stormtroopers?) in an enormous battle, we have hundreds of Jedi vs. the battle droids and some creatures. Yoda we have talk funny and butt kick with his light saber we do. We have Obi-Wan and Anakin speeding through the skies of Coruscant looking for a Bounty Hunter. And we have Obi-Wan vs. Jango Fett on the ocean planet of Kamino. It's all a lot of fun that the critics forget to easily.

However the scenes on Naboo with Anakin and Amidala aren't as good as the love scenes in TESB. The writing and directing is very mediocre here. But you sense the foolishness of youth here. They lack maturity and are getting married after having only been with each other for maybe a month at the most. On the other hand, the scenes on Tatoinee are great. You finally get a sense of the anger building within Anakin, especially when his mother dies and he kills a bunch of Tuskin Raiders, even the women and children. However, it's interrupted when they leave to rescue Obi-Wan.

So now we only have one Star Wars film left, ever. I think AOTC is a great preview of what's to come. After TPM, I was pleased, but had no desire to see the next one right away. After this one, I wish I could walk in to the next movie theater over and see Episode III. It's a great show that should be on everyone's summer movie list.

title: Dull as Dishwater
review:
Perhaps it's just me. I was in my teens when in 1977 Star Wars was released, and I found myself swept up in it completely. I first saw it in a provincial cinema in Lil' old England and audiences cheered out loud at the opening scenes, and continued to buzz through the whole movie. I have the original three on VHS and again on Laser and watch them regularly, and show them to my kids - who love them.

The contrast for AOTC could not be greater. I saw it today at a major Cinema in London and despite the digital presentation with superb picture and sound I struggled to stay awake for the first hour and a half, and then just about gave up. By the time the movie woke up I was out for the count, and wondering why I'd taken so much time out of my day to travel into town.

All prequels have to tie in to the stories that will follow (have followed?!) but Lucas seems to have laboured in a straightjacket trying to match plotlines in some instances, while driving a coach and horses through others. Forgive the ***spoiler*** here, but quite how C3PO can be owned by the same individuals on two separate occasions without either party having any memory of that is perhaps beyond belief.

The effects? Well I'm sure they'll give the graphics artists at ILM a decent showreel for their next job, but they added nothing to the entertainment.

This movie is a turkey, worse than the Phantom Menace, and Lucas can only improve on what will thankfully be his last attempt to inflate his bank balance at the honest moviegoers expense - at least with the Star Wars franchise.

title: A treat for all you Jedi Masters out there !
review:
Pure and simple: This is the best sci-fi movie to come down the pike in a LONG time. In fact, since 1980. (The Empire Strikes Back.) Attack of the Clones has faced paced battles, chases, duels, and the greatest FX seen in film to date! I won't give you a sypnosis, you can get that anywhere. Instead I'll tell you exactly why you should see this movie. First and foremost, the movies climax shows us The Battle of Genosis, an engagement that makes Hoth look like peanuts. With literally tens of thousands of droids and clones, this is the first real star WAR. The performances save those of Portman and Christanson are all good. Also, the supporting cast is all given significant screen time.

9/10 Stars

review:

title: Lucas can no longer direct
review:
Seeing this movie on the midnight showing was possibly the biggest waste of sleeping time I could ever imagine. I loved the original trilogy, and have never met a person that didn't. It was fun, it was engaging, and more importantly...I could believe it. In 2003, however, George Lucas has a bottomless pit of a wallet, and can shell out all he needs...to make this horrible, repeat...HORRIBLE movie. I thought, as would every fan, that Lucas would listen to the mistakes he made from the first. No, actually, he ignored them. Altogether, ignored them...and made a film equally bad, even if Jar Jar only makes a slight appearance as opposed to a full fledge role (a casting mistake from the start). First of all, because I do have basis, is CG. Computer graphics. Why is this a bad thing? Fake. It all looks amazingly...FAKE. I believe that I saw maybe one scene with C-3PO in a real, original trilogy, man in a metal suit, C-3PO suit. From there on? CG. In fact, Lucas decided that C-3PO is so amazingly cute, that he allows the droid to catch a 75 MPH hovering repair car by his hands in midair. We're talking, the same droid that could barely hold onto a wrench in A New Hope. Everything in the movie looks so unbearably fake. Lucas seems to have totally misused his position and vision, to give us 2 full length, badly scripted cartoons (the scripting was THAT bad. No scene took itself seriously, and was hardly believeable). The same ships, troops, and machines we found so amazing 20-25 years ago are now pale, cartoonish, and convenient. By convenient, I mean that the realistic, battle worn fighters that maneuvered their hearts out in the original series now conveniently zip around the screen like it's no big deal. Luke was a Jedi, and a damn good pilot, and even he can't make his ship double it's speed whenever he deems it convenient. Battles were horrible, paced was too fast (especially if you compare them to the long drawl of a buildup), and never got to the heart of it where we found ourselves so comfortable. In Jedi, we found ourselves a part of the action. It was dramatic and wild and engaging. Now, we barely get a chance to catch a glimpse of the action. Impersonal invasions by millions of CG (once again, the CG curse looms on) troops are barely followed, and if they are, it's too fake looking to buy.

Basic thing I'm trying to get across here is that this movie is a CG joke. Starship Troopers looked the same, only it had blood and made you at care at least a LITTLE bit. Somebody got their hands on a computer and had fun with it. Too horrid of a script that didn't take itself seriously. And oh yes, if you want proof that this movie is a joke, my entire theatre laughed insultingly when Yoda decided to drop his cane, draw a lightsaber, and bounce off the walls like he was Spider-Man (which is by far, going to beat Star Wars, if people have enough sense to ignore the hype of Episode 2). Lucas cannot direct anymore. Don't give him the money to make us wait in line on a Thursday night when we have to get up and go to work the next morning. Besides, at least you don't dream in CG.

title: Good movie, but not so good "Star Wars" episode.
review:
Possible spoilers ahead.

I'm not a fan of Star Wars, just fan of good movies.. AOTC as a movie was good. Great special effects, action, plot, characters. I'd say go see it, definitely.. I'd give it 7 stars. However, as a Star Wars movie, there were significant disappointments. +Special Effects: The effects in this movie were excellent. Lots of creativity went into character, costume, and background design, as a Star Wars movie should be. The different worlds that were shown were filled with a lot of details. One scene reminded me of a chase scene from Fifth Element..though..

+Action Scenes: The fight scenes, whether they were between Jedis or drones, clones, machines, space ships, they were all great. It's hard to beat a Star Wars and George Lucas on that.. I hate to repeat what everyone already said, but Yoda's scene was excellent.

-Anakin: I tried to like this character. I tried to have compassion for this poor kid (with all the bad things happened to him). But I couldn't. Although Vader's character was evil (until the very end), I had respect for him as the bad guy. I just can't imagine whiny Annie becoming the Vader character. I wished that they made him someone who I could like.. someone who I'd hate to lose to the darkside, but no.. not this kid.. the dark side can have him. Also the tragic scene with the death of you know who.. too cliche.

+Amidala: I thought Portman as Amidala was great. She makes a good Amidala.

-Romance: This was significantly disappointing. When Amidala says she love him, I was not convinced at all. Anakin had a crush on her at best.. was I expecting too much? Some of the lines were down right corny.. man they need better writers.

+/- Plot: The plot is very important, since they can not leave holes.. we know what happens later. In order to tell the story, you have to explain the important subplots and the origins or all the characters. This led to the film jumping around quite a bit.. but I thought it was a bit choppy.. I thought LOTR had done a better job telling its story.

Overall, I think acting and writing could've been much better. The pace could've been better too.. the first 2/3 was a bit too long to wait for all of the action. It was a good movie to see for the familiar plot, characters, and its excellent visual effects.. but now, I'm not so eager to see the next one.

title: Impressive. Most impressive.
review: For me, and I hope for many others, Attack of the Clones completely satisfied my every need for a film to be as fantastical and fresh as Lord of the Rings: FotR. I really believe that Lucas is growing better as a storyteller and a filmmaker and AotC proves this. It is much more confident and ambitious as The Phantom Menace and contains some of the greatest moments in the ever-evolving Star Wars universe.
