Even if some people cannot view that in the movie they can see the magnificent visual and audio show that stays in your mind even after the movie end. Memorable scenes that stay in your mind in a world of fast food-like-movies is something very precious and defining of the quality that this movie has.

In terms of the acting I'm forced to agree that for the time being the group of actors of the last movies don't seem as good as of the first set of movies, but again my opinion is that the lines and characters played in the first set of Star Wars didn't had much of a saying in terms of actor-like-movie and truth is that they didn't get prized by their acting in that first set so why should it be any different in the second set of SW. Maybe some people were seeing the movie only to catch the flaws and mistakes but that was not my case so I think the acting is very good taking in account that they were trying to enforce the role of events really would led to all the bad things that are supposed to happen in third chapter of this story. I must say that the romantic scenes and the acting of Hayden Christensen are very good and I believe that the scenes around Anakin relation with Amidala were very important to understand why will Anakin turn to the dark side (watch for next chapter). In this sense I think that this set of SW is much more developed in terms of personal stories than the first set were it seemed like the characters were less important to complete the story.

Finally I wish to say that SW II is a very impressive set of cinematic art and that it's good that people talk about it, good or bad critics.

title: About the dialogue
review:
First, let me just say that I enjoyed this movie a lot, not quite on the level of Episodes IV, V and VI, but I enjoyed it a bit.

But I have to complain about the dialogue, and more specifically about the people asserting that "the dialogue stunk in the first three movies too."

Ahem. The dialogue in the first three movies most certainly did not stink. This movie doesn't have anything that approaches the level of dialogue from various points in the first three movies, such as:

Han: I thought you liked scoundrels. Leia: I don't...I like nice men. Han: I'm a nice man. (kisses her)

Ben: Just myself, the boy...two droids...and no questions asked. Han: What are you, in some kind of local trouble? Ben: Let's just say we'd like to avoid any IMPERIAL entanglements.

Han: Listen, I had everything under control until you let us down here! Luke: Could be worse. (large rumbling noise) Han: It's worse.

Darth Vader, at the opening of ROTJ to Commander Jerjerrod: I hope so, Commander, for your sake. The Emperor is not as FORGIVING as I am.

Anyway, the dialogue in the first trilogy just had a better sense of playfulness; these people seemed like people. Even out in the middle of space, Han Solo and Luke Skywalker seem like regular people, as does Obi-Wan Kenobi, even if he comes across as a little sad. The characters here mostly serve plot rather than acting like people; as much as the effects and plot contributed to the success of the first three movies, the comradery between Han, Leia, Luke, Chewie, Lando & the Droids really shaped how we felt about these movies; they seemed like a family of people who we could admire and be friends with. Han & Luke seemed like friends. That comradery hasn't been established in I and II - Obi-Wan & Anakin don't have a particularly strong relationship, and Anakin & Amidala come across as forced more than anything else (save for the Gladiator scene, when the 3 more or less come together.)

title: Welcome to the Darkside
review:
Episode 2 is the fifth Star Wars movie. I remember seeing the original at the cinema (first release) and being blown away. However, I had seen Close Encounters' three to four weeks earlier and thought it was the better film. This feeling has only grown over the years. The Star Wars trilogy was not the best ever but were good family entertainment. This could never be said of The Phantom Menace', but early reviews had said that Clones' was much better, so with an open mind and three pints in my stomach off I trooped to watch the next instalment.

Anakin Skywalker, now twenty years old, is strong with force'. This power is beginning to corrupt him, as absolute power always will. The Sith (the bad guys) are growing in influence as Palpatine now heads up the Republic and Jedi membership, much like the priesthood, seems to be waning. Someone tries to assassinate Senator Amidala and much in love Anakin must play protector while Obi-Wan Kenobi tracks down those behind it.

I am going to try and restrain myself in this review, don't want to get carried away.

This is not a good film. It is visually STUNNING! Breathtakingly gorgeous. And the sounds of the ships etc. were fab. Deep thrums all over the place, and I like a deep thrum. Subwoofers going ten to the dozen, brill.

However, this is a film lacking any substantial story or plot. It appears to me that the premise of Episodes 1 & 2 is purely to show us how Anakin became Darth Vader. Not a strong enough plot for three movies. In episode 2 we have two weak and uninvolving stories occurring at the same time, which leads to a very thin, patchy and bity feel.

George Lucas as a Director is to be commended. The look of the film is wonderful. The CGI lets him down on a couple of occasions, but that is very picky. Yodas fight scene is just something to wonder at.

The actors do there level best, like the Director, to do whatever they can with the script. Hayden Christensen is good as the petulant adolescent. Ewan McGregor, Samuel Jackson and Christopher Lee are wasted. At no point are they ever given anything that is worthy of their talents.

The problem with this movie is at its core, the script. It is awful. Not only do we have these two stories interfering with the flow of the other, but the actual writing, the dialogue is simply terrible. The romantic scenes between Anakin and Amidala set a new level for cringe induction. George Lucas should never be allowed to write another script..ever.

People will say that I am expecting too much from what is essentially a kids movie. I say that I can still watch The Empire Strikes Back' and enjoy it. Lucas is living off of past glories and gullible filmgoers. That is the most annoying thing. When we have low budget, good films like Dog Soldiers' doing the rounds, it will still be hyped rubbish like this takes in the money.

title: As good as it gets
review:
Being a huge Star Wars fan I've been looking forward to Attack of the Clones. And I've got to say, I wasn't disappointed.

In a lot of ways this movie is a throwback to episodes four, five and six. The plot is interesting and flows along nicely, and it has a much darker and more complex feel that The Phantom Menace. In addition, it has very few appearances by Jar Jar Binks, and it brings back that great comedy double act of R2D2 and C3PO.

Overall the acting is very good. Hayden Christensen does a really good job, especially considering the character baggage he has to adopt. Natalie Portman and Ewan McGregor both put in great performances, as do Samuel L. Jackson, Christopher Lee and Ian McDiarmid. The script is a bit weak in places, but that is a known problem with George Lucas movies. It is certainly no worse that The Phantom Menace in that department.

The special effects and action sequences are awesome. The light sabre fights, the hover car chase, the land battle scenes, the space fighting scenes. There are so many of them that the movie generally keeps moving very well. There are a few slow spots (mainly involving Anakin and Padme's romance), but they are minimal and are necessary to the overall plot development. The storyline has obviously been very carefully thought out and really sets the scene for the later films.

I really enjoyed The Phantom Menace, but it wasn't quite up there. In my opinion this movie is right up there with episodes four, five and six. While it doesn't have the character chemistry that episodes four five and six had (courtesy of Hamill, Ford, and Fisher), it has its own good qualities and virtues. It is set in a different era and as such it shouldn't have to be a carbon copy of the other three.

And for all you Star Wars purists who keep slamming the prequels, why don't you do yourself (and the rest of us) a favour and avoid seeing them. If you are convinced that Lucas has ruined the trilogy I can guarantee you won't like this movie. Why? because it's not exactly like four, five and six, and when you leave the theatre you won't have physically turned back into a kid/teenager. But the truth is no matter how he could have done it you people wouldn't have liked it, so you may as well just save your money and your time.

For the rest of us, I strongly recommend this movie.

title: Lucas is back!
review:
I must confess, I was not as critical of George Lucas when I watched "Episode I" but I did think he'd lost his edge. It just lost some of the mystique of the original trilogy.

It had something to say for it: Natalie Portman (who we all fancied in "Leon" and were thoroughly ashamed of ourselves!), Darth Maul was moody and menacing and Ian McDiarmid did a brilliant turn, reprising his role (the only one to do so, except Anthony Daniels and Kenny Baker as the Droids) as the sinister Palpatine, presenting us with the roots of the Emperor's insidious rise to power. However, there were a number of major problems that can be summed up in three words: Jar Jar Binks.

Jar Jar was the epitome of everything that was wrong with Lucas' vision of "Episode 1", thankfully that George Lucas is dead and the Lucas we all knew and loved seems to have returned.

"Episode II" is a master stroke, returning to the mythological roots of the original trilogy. Dealing with intense political intrigue, "Episode II" sees the now retired Queen Amidala (a novelty for us Brits) acting as a controversial Senator Padme Amidala. Palpatine is now Supreme Chancellor of the Republic, which is under threat from a group of separatists led by the Count Dooku, played by Hammer Horror "Dracula" star and the old colleague of Peter Cushing (who played Grand Moff Tarkin in "Episode IV"), Christopher Lee. When an assassination attempt is made on Senator Amidala's life the Supreme Chancellor calls in the Jedi to protect her and Jedi Masters Mace Windu (Samuel L. Jackson is back and bigger than ever) and Yoda (voice of Frank Oz) assign the task to the now qualified Jedi Knight Obi-Wan Kenobi (Ewan McGregor continuing his transformation into Sir Alec Guinness) and his grown up padawan Anakin Skywalker (Hayden Christiansen taking over from Jake Lloyd).

This next installment in the Star Wars saga is mind-blowing. Lucas has assembled a characteristically brilliant cast, playing an array of highly imaginative new characters as well as some old favourites. Jar Jar Binks, now a representative in the Galactic Senate, is given a back-seat in this film, thank heaven. Top prizes go to Samuel L. Jackson and Ewen McGregor. Hayden Christiansen is brilliant as the angry young Skywalker and the sadly underrated Ian McDiarmid retains his brilliantly accomplished sleazy politician look. However, top marks must go to Christopher Lee as Lucas' new villain, picking up where Darth Maul left off after he 'split' in "Episode I". Count Dooku/Darth Tyranus is dark, mysterious and terrifying and Mr. Lee's excellent performance justifies my on-going calls for his knighthood!

You'll be wanting to see this again before it's even finished. The settings and characters are lavish and the battle scenes are simply amazing and you'll be completely gob-smacked by Yoda. Don't take your eyes off him if you want to see him kick arse. You won't believe it's the same Yoda.

I think Lucas has accomplished something I thought was impossible here: he's made up for "Episode I". Some of the love-scenes between Anakin and Padme are a bit syrupy and sicky but Lucas makes up for this by pulling off his attempts at humour by abandoning Jar Jar Binks in favour of some good old traditional C-3P0/R2-D2 slap-stick!

My only other criticisms would be that once again Lucas is relying too heavily on the special effects. Part of the brilliance of the original trilogy is that it all looks more real because they're models, not computer generated space ships, and the models are REAL! I was disappointed to see that Yoda was always computer generated. Maybe I'm just weird, but I liked the 'muppet', although it does make Yoda more flexible, which you'll all appreciate later on.

8/10

title: Black/white story with graphics that need more maturity
review:
I'm not sure if this is true, but I believe that Mr. Lucas said at some point that he hadn't done movies 1-3 first because of the fact that the technological advances in film making weren't yet at the level that he needed to make these movies.

Given that statement, and after seeing this movie, I have the feeling he should have waited a few years, still. Yes, the graphics are state of the art and much better than what we saw before. However, if you look at scenes, you will notice that each time only a certain set of colors is used, rather than the whole spectrum (which you would see in a normal movie, recorded on film rather than digitally). I'm not an expert on computer graphics, but I have the feeling that the color was removed from the recorded images, to allow the computer generated graphics to blend in better: without removing colors and enhancing the other colors, the computer generated parts would stand out too much. I had the same feeling while watching "The Lord of the Rings - The fellowship".

There are more similarities with "The Lord of the Rings". They both end at an odd moment (as they are both movies that have a planned sequel). They both are based on the 3D video game culture that exists nowadays (in fact, both movies might have been much more effective as a video game). They both make a clear distinction between "good" and "evil", with only rare attempts at creating a character that is in between (Boromir/Anakin), but not without giving the audience ample notice of this "anomaly".

I'm not saying it is a bad movie, but if you want to be awed by the graphics, it might be wiser to consider "Ice Age" or "Shrek". As for a better story line, I won't make suggestions for that, but there are plenty of movies in this database that have more depth. If you just want to see how the Star Wars hexology comes together, you should watch this movie, however.

title: Attack of the Mid-afternoon nap
review: It was there, in that plush representation of a vintage chair that I glided into a mid-afternoon slumber, as images of two dorks floundering in a flowery meadow and riding a elephant-beetle-beast-thing flashed infront of my closed eyelids. I thought Episode II was a complete disaster, even worse than the first one. Lucas blew several opportunities to display graphic violence for scenes of lush meadows and stormy seas. What this movie needed was an edge, and only the type of edge that the monumental and legendary actor Billy Drago can deliver. At least he could have saved the film. This movie isn't dark because it is negative and warlike, it is dark because everyone falls asleep while watching it.  Episode III better well be violent as hell (because of this supposed war that is supposed to be happening) or else I will be forced to finally conclude that Lucas is catering to all the little Kiddies out there in theater land. Why can't he make movies like Episode IV, where Spock dies and Robert or whatever his name is has to go and save him from the hideous, flame-throwing monster?

title: Visually Stunning - Pure SciFi
review: This movie more than makes up for Episode I - The Phantom Menace. You will be impressed. The scenery and visual/special effects are breathtaking. The only negative thing about this movie is the poor acting by Portman and Christiansen. Oh well... I'd sit through their drivel again to SEE the movie. Is there any way to watch it with the sound turned off? =)

title: Lots of Fun!
review: What can I say that you have not heard before?  This movie is a lot of fun and fills in many gaps between all the movies.  The special effects are fantastic and I really enjoyed the story.  Lets just say that I cannot wait for Episode III.

title: better than Episode I...
review:
CAUTION ** SPOILERS **

After watching this movie for the second time in 2 days, I have determined one very important note: These trilogies cannot be compared. The technology used in developing the new star wars films differs on such a large scale from the technology 25 years ago that it is an injustice to compare the two sets of films. Having that been said, Attack of the Clones is slightly less than what i had expected.

At times during the action scenes I kept having to remind myself that this IS a movie. Some of the action just seems over the top, without any consequences being thought of. For example, there is a scene in which a droid has placed posionous in senator Amidala's room in an assasination attempt. Obi-wan bursts into the room and jumps through the window, grabbing ahold of the droid as it pulls away from the window. Oh, i forgot to mention the droid is hovering 100 stories above ground. My only question is, what if the droid moved 2 feet to the left, or self destructed? SPLAT, no more Obi-wan. But for the sake of "the force" and hollywood, I'll stop asking questions and continue. Obi-wan then is saved when Anakin hops into a random speeder(unlocked, no keys) and rushes to his safety. Thats one count of Grand Theft Spacecraft, 10 years in prison. Anakin performs a similar suicide jump, jumping out of the moving speeder and landing on top of another moving speeder stories below.

The battles near the end were pretty nice, the CGI scenes FAR FAR more believable and less cartoonish than Episdoe I.

At times the movie seems to beg for a laugh,throwing out lame little one liners like C3PO with "what a drag" and "I'm beside myself." When will they realize that such comedic relief is not necessary.

Acting was also much better than Episode I, and solid in general. At times when Hayden Christensen seemed shakey, Natalie Portman was right there level it out again. Ewan McGregor, Natalie Portman, Ian McDiarmid, Christopher Lee all gave convincing performances in their roles. Christensen like I said seemed a bit shakey at times, but overall was pretty good, and expressed the forbidden Jedi emotions well.

My main grievance was the romance between Anakin and Padme. While it held such great potential, in my opinion it fell short. The character Anakin takes an almost stalker like approach; I need you, I love you, you are my soul, I'm dying when I know I can't be with you, etc. Secondly, she shows hardly any signs of loving him through most of the movie. And after psychotic episodes Anakin goes through, i.e. muderous rampages, she somehow sees past that and finds his inner evil creature, awwwww. You know how you try to force two jiggsaw pieces together even though you know they are no the right fit? Well that sums up the awkward and unlikely love between Anakin and Padme. Guys, believe me, if you are trying to win over a chick, Anakin's method DOES NOT WORK. I don't want to be the one who says I told you so, so please don't ever recite that speech to a REAL girl.

7 / 10 :better love story would have made this one a classic

title: All that money and can't write a decent script.
review: First off let me state i am not a huge star wars fan. However I love ESB, but loathed TPM. This one is a vast improvement from TPM which IMO was one of the worst "blockbusters" i've seen. This movie was going to sink or swim based on the romance, and sadly it sinks quicker than Demi Moore's movie career. The effect were great, but with that much money how could they not look great. I am beginning to hate movies with CGI in them because thats all the creators are worried about.... look how pretty that city looks screw the small scenes. I know the big debate is star wars or Spiderman, and i have to say spiderman triumphs where star wars fails the small scenes. These are the scenes that make a movie very good or can leave a movie (like this one) seemingly flat and fake. George spend some money and have a good screenwriter like Lawrence Kasdan (who helped write ESB and ROTJ) flesh out a better script. I want to like these movies but thats two movies in a row with my thumb pointing to the ground. 5/10

title: The Critics Have Failed Us
review:
Attack of the Clones is a good movie. All of the critics who have reconsidered (justifiably) their past positive reviews of Phantom Menace are taking it out on Episode II.

Attack of the Clones is a good, entertaining movie possessing many more positives and none of the negatives of Phantom Menace (which I will now state clearly, was not a good movie). Phantom Menace was racist (through ignorance rather than intention), juvenile and merchandise-based. Attack of the Clones is none of that.

Clones is a genuine Star Wars movie. It captures the essence of the originals, adds a dark twist and paves the road for a fantastic episode III (probably with an equally silly name). It undid the damage Phantom inflicted on Lucas's fan base and went beyond that. It fleshed out a mythology and story line with vibrant characters, plot and yes (though secondary in my mind) special effects (for those unable to experience DLP the first time, it is definitely worth a second or third viewing...at least).

This is a four star Star Wars movie.

title: Awful: Total lack of restraint
review:
I went to see EpII with an open mind, despite having been utterly dissapointed with Ep I. After all, Ep IV, V, and VI were all pretty good (teddybears not withstanding).

There is no doubt that Attack of the Clones is indeed better than The Phantom Menace. Unfortunately, it was still a terrible movie. Lack of restraint seems to be George Lucas' biggest problem (even more of a problem than his inability to write dialogue that doesn't induce vomit).

We have endless effects scenes, including the BladeRunner / Fifth Element section which had a plausability factor of zero. And then we had the whole section in the droid factory which added nothing, helped ensure that disbelief was utterly unsuspendable, and looked like a computer game. Threepio has his head welded onto a battle droid and the battle-droid has his head welded onto threepio (the same threepio that was built by a 7 year old boy...). I presume that was intended to be humour, but it all adds to the list of things which make the film unbelievable, and therefore ultimately pointless.

Obviously, the film had little or no consistency. Artoo now has little rocket thrusters and an fly around. Cool.... But hang on, this one is before EP IV, V and VI, so shouldn't he have been able to fly on those films too. That way he wouldn't have had to sink into that swamp....

The romance section reminded me of both Little House on the Prairy and the Sound of Music. A lot of people laughed at that point. My partner went to sleep.

The pity of it is, that with 20 - 30 mins of the retsraint-lacking (or just plain embarassing) scenese removed, it would probably be a half decent Star Wars film.

Finally, neither Portman or Christensen seem to be able to act. Which is unfortunate.

I'd like to think that Ep III is going to be better, but I have little faith.

title: The best experience I've had in a cinema!
review:
The Phantom Menace was a great film, despite widespread comments on Jar Jar. Believe it or not it wasn't about Jar Jar, it was meant to re-introduce us to the Star Wars galaxy and introduce the key characters to us. It did this and so much more brilliantly!

When I first heard of Attack Of The Clones I got very excited, the message to Obi-Wan Kenobi about the clone wars echoed in my head. So for the first time ever I go to see the film on the opening screening (Midnight), and everyone was excited! The audience (which included myself) would cheer at various points in the movie, and it is always so good to feel that shared excitement in a film!

The film is set 10 years after The Phantom Menace, and we see things in a new light. The special effects were great, so were stunts. I was very interested in finding out who the clones were, seeing 3PO's first flight into space and of course Jar Jar's blatant stupidity!

On the down side, and the only thing I can really comment against is the saber effects. Every so often in the film, you'll see a saber and it won't look as authentic as it did in the original trilogy.

Overall it was a WONDERFUL film. 10/10, and I'm tempted to say the best Star Wars film yet. But I've only seen it once, the movie won't be quite so grand the second time around :)

-Daniel

title: Better than Episode One--but takes itself too seriously
review:
I actually debated whether or not I would EVER see this film, after the trailers seemed heavily weighed in the romance direction, but seeing an advance screening convinced me that there is still hope for the franchise.

Not as weighed down by exposition as was Episode One, ATTACK OF THE CLONES still suffers the great fault of the first film: It just takes itself too seriously. Within ten minutes, I felt as though I were embroiled in some game of Dungeons and Dragons, the techno-jargon and suspicious whispering that have replaced the casual banter of the original trilogy (where, oh where, has Han Solo gone?) were almost enough to make me regret my decision to buckle in for the full two and a half hours. But then, wonder of wonders, I got caught up in a chase scene in which Obi Wan and Anakin get to show off their ridiculously super-Jedi powers and, gasp!, some off-the-cuff chit-chat!

In short, the romance stuff is awful, though not as embarrassing as good ol' Jar-Jar, whose cameos are blessedly brief. As you've no doubt heard, it's time for Yoda to shine, and for us to learn about the parts of Anakin's past that are going to get him into the black mask. Sure, a lot of it is heavy handed, but I think all six films fall under that criticism--mythology isn't the most subtle of genres.

Be prepared for the appearance of characters you may have been waiting for...and some other surprises (one of which, regarding R2-D2 in a scene out of INDIANA JONES AND THE TEMPLE OF DOOM, I found to be something of a cheat). And if the guy sitting next to you is laughing at dialogue you may not find funny, take some advice I wish Georgie Lucas would listen to: Lighten up. It's a movie, not a science. That's why we love it, and that's why we're asking for more.

title: I'm Back on Board The Star Wars Love Train
review:
Episode I derailed my almost unshakable faith and love for the star wars universe. It's funny actually, because I didn't hate Episode I, it just got old for me... I wanted more, and I felt Lucas dropped the ball. Jar Jar was disappointing as a whacky alien sidekick, and made chewbacca's wookie light shine even brighter. Now that I think about it, Jar Jar is a permanent skidmark on my darth vader underoos, and I say that with conviction.

However, Episode II is absolutely heads above Episode I, and may even break into the rankings of the original series. I think comparing the two series is a terrible trap to fall into, though, so I won't travel down that road. There's simply too much nostalgia with the original series... and I hold the first three films far too dear to my heart to make a fair comparison.

AOTC delivers on several fronts, and faulters (but doesn't collapse) on a few others. The FX are what you would expect, and the dialogue is... sigh... also what you would expect, but that ultimately doesn't matter much. If the storyline to AOTC was a woman, it would be a real sexy vixen. The plot is well developed and executed, and since a good story is undoubtedly a powerful ally, it makes even the most mediocre

acting passable, as long as it advances the plot. I can't think of one scene (even the love scenes) that i would consider unnecessary or superfluous. That's a really important point to make, and I think even the film's detractors would agree with me on that point. Hayden

Christensen's portrayal of Anakin is solid, and Ewan Mcgregor really begins to fill out the role of Obi-Wan Kenobi in this installment.

Natalie Portman seems a little too diametric with her acting: at some points she's stiff, at others completely at home with the role. C3PO turns into a veritable comedic whore unfortunately, but still manages to pull off a few memorable quips. Christopher Lee is spectacular in this chapter, and is a very, very welcome addition to the growing fold of star wars actors. In a sense, his character completely makes the movie for me, especially when he's on-screen with yoda (wink wink).

This is how it all pans out:

Ups.

1. Story Line, Story Line, Story Line.

2. Christopher Lee's Count Dooku and Ewan McGregor's Obi-Wan

3. Awesome FX and a completely beautiful and superbly realized worlds.

4. Yoda.

5. The avoidance of complete butchery of the romantic subplot.

6. Oodles of action.

7. Mace Windu.

Downs

1. Stiff acting from portman and less frequently, from christensen.

2. Whoring of C3PO as a Jar Jar standin during the climax.

3. Jango's destruction was a bit too simple, but badass nonetheless.

Either Ors

1. Did Obi-Wan kick enough ass? Questionable.

2. A little short on humor?

3. Yoda's dialogue a little... unnatural? Odd delivery?

You decide.

In the grand scheme of things, AOTC is a true winner and a great film. I refuse to rank it, but tend to feel that it's far superior to

Episode I in about every aspect possible.

Do See. A-.

title: Great movie in spite of the director. . .
review:
Star Wars is a critic-proof saga. This is because George Lucas took a generation when they were young and captured their imaginations, passion, and interest with a story that had action, drama, mystery, all in a universe of his own design. Approximately 25 years after Star Wars: A New Hope, we have the fifth movie, the second of the story that has now a built in audience of grown-ups who like to reminisce about their child-hood. Yes, I am one of these. And not matter what the critics said, I was determined to see it opening day.

To be honest, the film is not as good as it could have been. This does not mean that it was bad or even mediocre, but it was the best it could've done with the talent in hand. Were the actors sub-par? No. Were the sets, the scenery, the props, the costume, unrealistic or even poorly constructed? No. Did the acting leave you feeling a bit emotionally detached from the characters? A bit.

Samuel Jackson, Ewan McGreagor, Natalie Portman, Christopher Lee, all of these human actors, Even Hayden, can give stellar performances. We've seen them all at their best, and this wasn't it. It's not their fault. Honestly, it's George Lucas. He just can't seem to direct. That's probably why everyone thinks Empire Strikes Back was so great; he left the directing to someone else. Yes, some of the dialogue was plastic, but it probably wouldn't have been as apparent it wasn't buttressed by the acting.

Attack of the Clones. Simple. To the point. B-movie title. I wish it was something else (i.e. The Clone Wars), but I'm not the one who came up with the idea so I didn't get to have my say. What can you do? Nobody's perfect.

So there's the down side of the movie. Now for the upside. ..

This movie had a lot in it. Visually there is more to take in than can possibly be absorbed in one sitting. The settings are wonderful. Even the barrenness of Geonosis has a splendor to it. The characters are more fluid (even Jar Jar) than Episode I.

The story has more development than the last film as well. Episode I, at some points seemed to never pick up the pace. That isn't the case with this movie. The movie starts with an explosion. The movie has a lot in it. There is actually some development. We are able to see what causes Anakin to start his dangerous trek to the dark side. We see a peaceful government loose control. We are introduced to new characters like Owen and Beru Lars, Boba Fett, who play key roles later on. We see Ewan's Obi Wan become more like Alec's. And on that note, there was one scene where Anakin and Obi Wan were looking for an assassin in a bar. Obi Wan stops and there is a close up on his face. You could almost see Alec Guinness.

So what is the film about? This movie is a lot about Anakin. After all, George says the saga is about Anakin more than it is about Luke Skywalker. It's about how we see him starting to turn to the dark side, even though he might not know it yet. It's about his struggle to submit to Obi Wan. This struggle includes his feelings for Padmé, which is forbidden in the Jedi Order.

However, this movie is also about how the Empire came into being. We know the end from the beginning. We can see how certain decisions made by key characters affect the rise of the Empire. Not that the Empire was created in Episode II, but we can see the seeds starting.

This movie is about the Jedi Order. We can see how arrogance is really the weakness of the jedi, be they on the light or dark side of the force. We see how this plays together in the fall of the Republic.

There is a lot of eye candy in this movie. The exotic creatures. The light saber fights. The large scale wars. How different jedi use the force. These are all eye popping and really keep the story going. But this is what Lucas is known for. His innovations with technology and creation of fantasy are unrivaled in this day and age.

Jar Jar is still alive. You probably think this should be another downside to the film, but his character is more toned down, even subdued. He has very little screen time and isn't as much of a comic relief as was attempted in Episode I. If this is how he was in the previous film, I'm sure there wouldn't be as much hatred for him as there is today.

So would I see it again? Most definitely yes. I enjoyed the story. With the idea in mind that Lucas isn't as great a director as he is a creator/story teller, it isn't as hard to look past the acting issue. Though the title can make you shudder with B-movie dread, it is a class A flick.

title: The Real George Lucas
review:
I, like many of my generation, grew up idealizing George Lucas. The seemingly brilliant mind behind Star Wars and Indiana Jones was an icon for me even into film school. However, with the second installment of the spiraling disappointments known as the Star Wars prequels, we're beginning to see that George Lucas is far from a genius filmmaker.

Let's start with Attack of the Clones. Here is a movie that further does the job of making something as dreamily cool as the Jedi Knights and makes them dull, lifeless characters. Attack of the Clones is the result of a man who has spent too long directing special effects and left the actors drifting on their own.

I was worried when I heard Episode II was being "filmed" entirely in digital format that the switch to video would leave the image lifeless, as is video's reputation. But, this movie has so much more wrong with it than the stock it was shot on, things wrong with it before it ever moved onto the movie set.

The "story" centers around the further political machinations of the Sith and the crumbling of the Republic brought up in The Phantom Menace. However, stories about a setting are not interesting and Mr. Lucas seems to have completely forgotten what made Star Wars so cool in the first place: characters.

So the characters that were thrust together by dubious plot devices in the first episode continue to adventure through the galaxy in this one, except for the annoying Jar Jar, who is mercifully underscored in this picture. Even boring characters such as these would have been better served to be together, but within the first thirty minutes of the movie, everyone goes their own way and the movie stops nearly all action in favor of lecturing you about the events transpiring.

At least in the previous trilogy, when the characters got separated, it was to interact with other characters. It serves as a poor reflection on this movie that the best character in the whole movie is a now computer generated Yoda.

Everyone finally reassembles in the drawn out third act, which boils down to the now standard Star Wars epic computer generated battle scenes. The largely unmotivated third act seems to be an attempt by George to sell video games and more toys. During the ending battle, seven or eight new varieties of vehicles (aka toys) show up for no plot-driven reason.

It is clear to me, now, that everything that made the original Star Wars trilogy what it was are gone: the late, great Joseph Campbell and budget limits. Joseph Campbell made Star Wars the modern myth it is today and the limits imposed on Mr. Lucas in the early days of Star Wars forced him to streamline and focus.

The point is, nothing I can say will sway you from seeing this movie. I'm sure you'll see it eventually if you already haven't, but please do not pay full price for it. George Lucas has finally come too close to the Saturday Matinee B-movie source material he treasured as a child.

title: A good movie, much better than Episode I
review:
This is probably the second best of all the Star Wars movies. Empire is definitely better, but this is better than "A New Hope." Regardless, it's a whole lot better than Episode I (which isn't saying much).

I watched the Episode I because, well it's the law. I watched it again to see if it was as bad as I thought it was, it was. That won't be true with Episode II.

Episode II starts out a little slow (and that's an understatement). With in the first few scenes you see Jar Jar, and think "oh crap, here we go again." The convoluted love scenes with Anakin and Padme are difficult, but not totally unbearable. Mixed in with a split story with Obi Wan, which makes it confusing to follow. The guy next to me was snoring like a lawn mower!

Second half is some of the best action I've ever scene, mixed in with excellent character moments. You literally get to watch Anakin move from an obnoxious, arrogant kid, to a deeply troubled young man (setting us up for a great episode III). I chewed through a straw in Empire, and if I had one here I would have done the same at some scenes in Episode II.

The only drawback with this movie is too much plot. The plot is like a James Bond movie, with 16 different locations. You're exhausted in the end. The excess if action plot doesn't allow for character development that the first (holy) trilogy has.

title: Definitely a Star Wars Film...
review:
I'm a Star Wars fan. I've seen all four previous films for the nth time (yes, even that dreaded Phantom Menace)... and what I can say about Attack of the Clones is it's a fun and enjoyable ride and I will definitely watch it again.

You guys might think that I only said this because I am a fan... maybe you're right. But hey, I've also repeatedly seen movies such as Lord of the Rings (which I think is still much better than any of the Star Wars films), Requiem for a Dream, and Hitchcock's Psycho and loved these films for what they are. I just think that sometimes you just have to look at at Star Wars movies for what they are... a kid/teen flick with all the high-tech mumbo-jumbo with not that much of a story.

Sure, dialogue's bad... as usual. Love scenes were not that believable but hey... who would believe that a not-that-experienced pilot (who's not yet a jedi) can channel the "Force" and shoot down a planet-sized Death Star with his pathetic X-wing?

I guess what I'm trying to point out is... I can't believe that people would say that AOTClones is a bad movie while claiming that IV, V, and VI are among the best sci-fi/adventure movies (Phantom Menace is an exception cause it's really bad! That's another 4 paragraphs that I won't discuss here). I believe that AOTClones lived up to being a Star Wars movie... people watching should just clear their minds of any preconceptions and let George take them to a place A Long Time Ago in a Galaxy Far, Far Away.

title: The best story is the one that everyone seems to miss
review:
**********SPOILERS*************

The best story is the one that everyone seems to miss. People seem to concentrate their attention towards the special effects and the flaws of the movie.

First, the flaws. I will admit, the dialogue is a bit cheesy at times, but Star Wars itself is a fantasy world and it is utterly impossible to make realistic dialogue in such an environment. Also, Heyden Christiansen is ok. Could be better, but he is MUCH better than Jake Lloyd. Other than that, no major complaints.

Now, the good parts. The parts that gave this movie the familiar Star Wars feel. George Lucas does a great job of leaving us hanging for the next one (3 years!), and forshadowing the fates we all know dooms each character.

First, the special effects are superb. While some are better than others, overall they are amazing.

The parts that most people missed were the subtle forshadows which Lucas has ingeniously placed into the movie. There is one "mystery" that if you look deep enough can be solved. That mystery is "Who placed the order for the clone army?" Now, the simple answer would be the Jedi that died 10 years ago. However, that is not correct. Darth Sidious placed the order under the Jedi's name so that he would have is own army. Everyone thought it would be for the Republice, but Sidious (Palpatine) and Dooku have other plans. They plan to split the Republic in two, and since Palpatine controls both sides he will have a grand army for what will be the Empire. They plan to turn Anakin to the Dark Side by convincing him that Obi Wan is holding him back and that he doesn't need guidance. Great plan, but Lucas is the one who conveys this so well.

Also, another sign of Lucas' brilliance is the scene when Anakin tells Amidala that he killed all of the Tusken Raiders. Then he said "I hate them." Keyword: hate. "Fear leads to anger, anger leads to hate, hate...leads to suffering." --Yoda. The little green Jedi master predicted it all. Anakin's FEAR of harm coming to his mother is realized, so he kills the Raiders. Then he HATES them. Next up: suffering. Also, when Anakin said "I hate them," the imperial music played (I didn't notice this until the second time I saw it). That is INCREDIBLE forshadowing.

In addition to predicting Anakin's fate, our little green Jedi proves to possess some other unknown skills. Yoda's knowledge of the Force is unmatched. And, a scene we've all been waiting for has finally come, Yoda duels with a lightsaber. Unbelievable! Awesome!

Overall, I give this movie a:

9/10 ***1/2 A-/A

It was a great film and a perfect addition to this already amazing saga. Much better than Episode I, it leads in nicely to the original 3. It provides some connections to what we already know, and others a mystery. I recommend this to people who know Star Wars at all, and to people who have already seen it so they can really appreciate the hints and messages that Lucas has left us.

title: as good as the originals
review: Just a quick note: this movie had groundbreaking effects, humor, spectacular action sequences, great characters, and visual images like none i have ever seen (just like the originals). title: Expectations not met, but a good movie nonetheless (Spoiler Warning)
review:
(Spoiler Warning ahead)Learning from past mistakes with the euphoria of the Phantom Menace, I took a cautious approach to viewing the Attack of the Clones. In every way it is a superior film to Episode One and not because it lacked Jar-Jar Binks and more Yoda. There is the blend of a continuation of a long story that is the Star Wars Saga as we know it along with the stump splitting war sequences we all grew up with in the Original Trilogy. However George Lucas, who several months ago suggested that there would be a lot of romance, smartly didn't push it so much towards the last month going into the release and rightly so; the romance was not believible due to his lack of letting his actors act, especially Natilie Portman. review: Alright im just going to get this out of the way, Aotc is better than phantom. ITs got a better story,better action, better effects and just plain more enertaining in my mind. title: Better than what some might lead to believe...
review:
Before I start, may I just point out to those who have blasted this film repeatedly to hear me out.

When George Lucus made the first Star Wars in 1977, he had the luxury of not having ten thousand movie critics waiting in line at the premier ready to confirm what everyone expected: that the movie did not live up to its predecessors. Now, 20 years after Return of the Jedi, Lucus is under the microscope after the failure of Menace. Can we all for once just sit back, eat our popcorn, and try to enjoy the movie without disecting it as we watch?

Attack of the Clones is no Citizen Kane, but it doesn't need to be. Star Wars is about entertainment, and Clones delivers it in full force. It's packed with many memorable action sequences, among others the amazing car chase on Coruscant and the Yoda/Dooku battle, and I can honestly say that I did not leave the theater feeling cheated. But then again, I didn't go in expecting to be which COULD have played a small part in that...

title: Not just Lucas, but Star Wars, too, is back.
review:
This is the most entertaining out of all the Star Wars movies. Lucas brings back the franchise where it belongs with loads of nostalgic hype and links to the originals. This may be a simply effective tool to reign the box office, but I think I stand with most Star Wars geeks in saying that those subtle and obvious foreshadowing points, etc. effectively brought huge grins on each person's face. On top of this, the visuals in the film are simply unparalleled. While Phantom Menace (which still is not a Star Wars movie in my book) had good stuff, the art was not so effectively implemented with the new visual technology as in this film. Every new amazing shot of a spaceship, and you think they will not be able to top it, and then the next one leaves you hyperventilating because the visuals are that awesome. The computer-generated character models are especially good--Jar-Jar looks even better than he did in Phantom, etc.

There aren't too many flaws in this film for actual movie quality. (There are none for entertainment value.) The dialogue in a few scenes, especially the romantic ones, can get really lame. Other times, though, the script is some of the best throughout all of Star Wars. Even still, looking back at the originals, there has always been some pretty poor dialogue once in a while, and that did not hamper them in any way, and ultimately ends up only as a one point drop on 10 scale, at most. Another problem was the presentation of Natalie Portman in a few scenes. She obviously has great acting talent, and the problem was not her. (Also, she is absolutely, constantly beautiful/sexy) But she was not given the regality from Phantom that many of the scene's scriptings still called for. The biggest one was a packing scene in which she kept stooping over, even when she needed to express her power, and the script doesn't really intend for her to appear so awkward throughout the scene. I originally felt that the plot did not move enough in this movie, it mostly just thickens, and there is a lot to be taken care of in the next one, but then my friend reminded me that Empire really did not move that much, either, so much as leaving us on a cliff-hanger, and Empire is the best of all Star Wars. So, the plot is fine overall. Other than that, not too many problems.

The good stuff. Surprises of all surprises, the character of Jar-Jar Binks has completely redeemed himself. I love the way he was used in this movie, for the deservedly short screen time he had. Ewan gives the great performance we always knew he could for Star Wars, but the script still limits him as compared to some of his more powerful performances. Natalie is good when presented correctly, and Samuel Jackson gives a basic, Steve McQueen-esque performance that has no fault but does not steal the spotlight (fortunately). Hayden Christensen is the man. Except when the scripting for him absolutely bites, he takes the cake for best performance in the movie, rivaling the quality in Star Wars of Harrison Ford and Billy Dee Williams (my personal favorites) A few scenes will have you gaping at just how good this guy is, and I hope many casters and producers will pick him up for more, because he can do it. Oh, and by the way, in case you had not heard it enough, Yoda = god. Basically, combine the great character he has always been, then take the level of coolness of the younger Marlon Brando, or maybe Shaft, and combine it with his philosophical character, and you have the freaking coolest thing in a really cool movie. The main bad guy is pretty cool, as well, but not as cool as his lightsaber.

Basically, the coolest part of this movie is the large battle sequence at the end. Easily the best in all sci-fi/fantasy ever, this battle is amazing, and I dare to say it rivals Black Hawk Down in actual movie quality of capturing the action. It is simply amazing, and perfectly done.

Lucas really treads some new, sweet ground in this with a totally sweet chase scene resembling noir stuff, and the realism-based epic battle. Overall, in actual movie quality I think this is better than Return, a little better than A New Hope (my second favorite) and almost touches Empire, even though by touching it it would not necessarily be as good. If the script for the romance sequences had been improved it would definitely touch Empire. By the way this movie headed, the next one could very easily beat Empire in quality, because so much great plot-stuff has to be taken care of.

See this as soon as you can, and then as many times as you feel are necessary to take in all the great details and entertainment. I plan to see it around four, maybe five times in theaters, and I rarely go out to see a movie. It is that good, and mostly because it is that fun.

(9/10)

title: Enjoyable, lacking plot
review:
First off, I'd like to answer everyone who's been comparing this and Episode I to the original trilogy. I've got big news for all you folks...those movies were made over twenty years ago! Sorry to say, but times have changed since then. George Lucas isn't an idiot...he knows exactly what he's doing, and he's making movies for today's generation. Episode I was childish, because it was made for mostly children. Episode II is a little more mature, because those kids are a little more mature now. And so on.

With that said, let me talk about the movie....

It's no masterpiece, but it was definitely enjoyable. Anyone looking for Oscar-calibre performances will not find it here (although I do admit, Hayden Christensen did a much better job than I expected). The Oscars suck anyways.

The thread of a plot centers mostly around young Anakin, his love for Padmé Amidala, and his short temper. The rest is about this mysterious Clone army, supposedly built for the Republic but was not authorized to (although Yoda makes magnificient use of them in the spectacular and very redeeming final sequence). And, of course, there's the evil Count Dooku (played disappointingly by Christopher Lee) and his army of Battle Droids. Conspiracies abound, including plans to construct the Death Star, etc., but I won't give away too much.

Anyway, besides the fact that the plot barely moves and it's mostly just a bunch of action sequences and political discussions strung together, I found this movie very confusing. Not to understand, just to look at. Maybe I was just too close to the screen or something, but I found there were just too many creatures and too many spaceships and too much happening at once to really concentrate on what was going on (maybe this was intentional...makes you want to go back and see it again to figure it all out). Some of the dialogue was cheesy, but that was expected.

Now back to Hayden's performance; it wasn't gold, but much, much better than I had thought it would be. He didn't seem like the little boy in the last film, but definitely like the young man who'll become Darth Vader (there's one gut-wrenching scene on Tatooine where he admits his slaughter of those barbaric sand people...nearly flawless). He certainly seems to keep the whole film together, as he should, since the whole film's about him.

One of my biggest problems with films these days are the special effects. Honestly, movies from the 80s or early 90s had better special effects than nowadays. Why? Because computer animation wasn't very developed yet, and they were forced to rely on things like models and animatronics, thankfully. I'm sorry, but CGI is just so obviously...CGI. It stands out so painfully from everything else, it just completely ruins the believability of the film. One frame can be photo-realistic, but an entire sequence? George Lucas, please, do it the old-fashioned way next time. I dare you. It worked great for the original trilogy (ahh, but that brings me back to my opinion on this being a trilogy for today's generation...however, i doubt they think CGI looks any more realistic than I do).

But I digress. This isn't a bad film, not by any means. It's a summer film...it's not one that'll leave you pondering life or anything, but it manages to get the major points across to set up for the next one, as Episode I did (much worse though). Don't expect any cinematic epic, but it is entertaining and well worth your money (more so than other movies coming out this summer, that's for sure). It will, however, leave you very p***ed off that we won't get to see Episode III for another three years.

All in all...I want to see it again.
